He earned first-team All-Ivy League honors in 2022 and was named a finalist for the Walter Payton Award as the top player in the FCS. He ranked ninth in that division with 118.3 yards per game, carrying the ball 206 times for 1,183 yards (5.7 per) and 10 touchdowns (also 5-58-11.6, one TD receiving) in 10 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Borguet is compactly built with a powerful base and an ability to power through arm tackles. While he displays pretty good vision and can get to his cuts once he’s past the line of scrimmage, a lack of suddenness and excessive dancing is likely to work against him versus NFL speed.
strengths: Compact and extremely powerful; cranked out 35 bench-press reps at pro day. | Runs with controlled strides for optimal power and balance. | Able to stack cuts together with relative success. | Drives feet through contact for additional yardage.
weaknesses: Tightness in his hips limits quick-cut agility. | Takes too much time to process the front. | Unable to dash away from tacklers after slowing his feet. | Not much of a factor in the passing game at Harvard.

bio: O'Connell did not start for Stevenson High School in Illinois until his senior year. He set school records with 2,471 passing yards and 26 passing touchdowns. He committed to Division III Wheaton College, but he decided to walk-on at Purdue instead. He did not play in 2017 or 2018 but started three of six games played as a redshirt sophomore (103-164-62.8%, 1,101 yards, eight TDs, four INTs). O'Connell started the first three games of the 2020 season (88-136-64.7%, 916 yards, seven TDs, two INTs) before missing the rest of the year with a foot injury. He stayed healthy in 2021, earning second-team All-Big Ten Conference honors and ranking third in the FBS by completing a school-record 71.8 percent of his passes (315-439, 3,712 yards, 28 TDs, 11 INTs) in 12 games with nine starts. O'Connell was a second-team selection again in 2022 (320-499-64.1%, 3,490 yards, 22 TDs, 13 INTs), starting 12 games before opting out of the team's bowl game to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: O’Connell’s 2021 tape is better than what we saw from him in 2022, but there were still flashes last season. He’s a pocket passer who can throw with solid accuracy over the first two levels but struggles with trajectory and rhythm on deep targets. O’Connell has below-average mobility inside and outside the pocket. He needs to keep his progressions on schedule and his throws on time to make up for average arm strength. He had to carry a heavy percentage of the offense on his back at Purdue and could benefit from an offense that allows him to manage games. O’Connell has backup potential and his upside is slightly above average.
strengths: Experience playing under center and in a pro-style system. | Stands tall in the pocket and delivers over the top. | Play-action throws feature good timing to the route. | Anticipatory passing makes up for a lack of velocity. | Good accuracy and placement throwing between the hashes. | Completion totals hurt by a high number of drops by receivers. | Willing to check it down and move on to the next play. | Makes attempts to get the ball out instead of taking a sack.
weaknesses: Slow, plodding feet in his pocket setup. | Staring at targets allows linebackers and safeties to get a jump on the throw. | Can be a little too stubborn in sticking with his primary read. | Rarely gets his back hip rotated through the delivery. | Sensitivity to pressure causes rushed read and ball delivery. | Average velocity leads to floating sideline throws. | Completed just 29.6 percent of his deep throws in 2022. | Leggy strides hinder ability to escape pocket peril.

bio: Ali started eight games (two at right guard, six at left guard) as a redshirt freshman at SMU, playing in 12 contests overall, after earning honorable mention All-Texas notice at Timber Creek High School. He moved to center for 2019, starting all 13 games that year and all 10 the following season. American Athletic Conference coaches voted him second-team all-league in 2021 even though he missed two games due to injury, as he started eight of 10 games played (first five at center, next two at left tackle, one at right tackle). Ali transferred back to his hometown of Fort Worth to play for TCU in 2022. He was a first-team All-Big 12 pick for the Horned Frogs, starting all 15 games at center during their run to the national title game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ali has limited size and length, but he plays with good consistency and the fortitude to give himself a chance in the league. Very quickly, the tape shows off his body control and core strength, which help him stay connected to blocks through adversity. A lack of length will put him in a hole against long-armed tackles, and he will need help handling odd front nose tackles. The pass protection is inconsistent and could stay that way due to a lack of physical traits. He might not get drafted, but he could surprise in a camp.
strengths: Keeps pad level low off the ball. | Hands stay tight and into opponent’s frame. | Drives from insteps to stay connected with the block. | Climbs to linebacker with patience and control. | Looks for additional work to clean up the front. | Punches with independent hands in pass sets.
weaknesses: Below average mass and length. | Could struggle to hang in against an odd front nose tackle. | Tackles with length can separate and shed him. | Can get lost against twists and delayed blitzes. | Short arms stymie ability to redirect an edge rush.

bio: Austin was a three-star recruit out of Long Beach Poly near Los Angeles. He redshirted his first season, playing in three games as a reserve (seven tackles, one pass breakup). Austin was a five-game starter in 2020 (29 tackles, two pass breakups in seven appearances) and then garnered honorable mention All-Pac-12 honors as a sophomore (47 tackles, two interceptions, seven pass breakups in 13 starts) and junior (57 tackles, one sack, two interceptions, one of which was returned for a touchdown, with 10 pass breakups in 12 starts) before declaring for the draft. Alex’s younger brother, Daylen, signed to play at the University of Oregon in 2023. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Austin’s size, length and football IQ work in his favor, but there is a lack of consistency with his man coverage that could limit the way NFL teams use him. He’s decent at mirroring the release from press but struggles to stay in-phase with quality route runners. He plays with below-average top-end speed and recovery burst in man coverage, but his instincts and awareness take him where he needs to go from off-man and zone coverage. Austin can play some press and a variety of zones and offers backup potential as a Day 3 option.
strengths: Angular cornerback with good length to challenge the throw. | Above-average ball production over the last two seasons. | Potential to play multiple zone coverages and bump-and-run. | Sinks into balanced zone positioning between routes. | Communicative in space and overlaps coverage to make plays. | Excellent field awareness of route combinations. | Cares about run defense and hustles from the back side.
weaknesses: Backpedal when matching release is a little bumpy. | Unable to swivel and recover when routes cross his face. | Loses ground against pure vertical routes. | Inconsistent staying in range of well-run routes from man. | Does too much leg diving and not enough wrap tackling after the catch. | Needs to come off blocks more quickly in run support.

bio: Forsyth was a four-star recruit at West Linn High School (Oregon) before driving south to Eugene for college. He redshirted the 2017 season before playing in five games as a reserve guard and tackle in the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Forsyth was named second-team All-Pac-12 as a junior in 2020, starting all seven games for the Ducks at center. In 2021, he started nine games but missed five others with a back injury, still garnering second-team all-conference accolades. He was a 2022 first-team all-conference pick and finalist for the Jason Witten Collegiate Man of the Year award, given to the CFB player who demonstrates outstanding leadership, courage, integrity and sportsmanship. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A steady center/guard option with good size and length, Forsyth plays with technique and consistency that offensive line coaches will appreciate. He wasn’t asked to play with much range from home base but gets into his block with pop and is consistent in his effort to sustain and finish the assignment. He has some issues protecting the A-gaps at times, and the pre-snap penalties are a concern. Forsyth’s poor explosiveness testing at the NFL Scouting Combine could cause concerns for teams looking at him late on Day 3 of the draft.
strengths: Fits into blocks with efficiency and pop. | Well-schooled and plays with inside hands. | Rolls hips into block and runs feet at contact. | Creates wash-down blocks out of defender’s momentum. | Sustains and finishes at the desired rate. | Pass sets with stiff left jab and good body control. | Opens hips and springs lateral to catch incoming twist.
weaknesses: Pre-snap yips turned into penalties. | Below average snap-to-step quickness protecting A-gap. | Might need additional core strength for NFL battles. | Very average range setting out to edge attacks. | Needs better hand resets to capture leverage against rusher.

bio: Palczewski (pal-CHESS-key) suffered a fractured vertebra in his neck as a junior in high school. He returned from the injury to become a top 50 offensive tackle prospect nationally from Prospect High School. He started the final 11 games of his true freshman season at guard (switching between left and right) for Illinois. Palczewski started all 12 games at right tackle in 2018 and then began all 13 games at that spot in 2019, garnering third-team All-Big Ten honors. He started four games at right tackle in 2020, missing the rest of the year with an ACL injury. Palczewski earned 2021 honorable mention All-Big Ten honors for his efforts in 12 starts (seven at tackle, five at guard). He started all 13 games at right tackle in 2022, tying the FBS record with 65 career starts as well as earning third-team Associated Press All-American and all-conference accolades. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Palczewski has played his fair share of football games. The experience shows with his poise and understanding of assignments on each snap. He’s quick out of his stance and does a nice job of making blocks in space, but lacks the functional power to sustain blocks against power on a consistent basis. He needs to get bigger and stronger to stick around in the league.
strengths: Comes out of his stance ready to strike. | Connects and triggers feet to sustain the block. | Very fluid making adjustments in space. | Stays in front of rusher with consistent mirror. | Able to slide quickly inside to meet counters.
weaknesses: Below average mass and width to his frame. | Leans into contact with his chest ahead of hands. | Struggles to maintain blocks against power players. | Gets bounced backward by speed-to-power rush. | Unable to redirect rush pressure through his edge. | Suffered knee and foot injuries during his time at Illinois.

bio: Pihlstrom (pronounced PILL-strum) signed with Illinois out of the Chicago suburb of Glen Ellyn, where he was an all-conference and Academic All-State selection at Glenbard West High School. He did not see the field as a redshirt freshman tight end in 2018 and then played in one game at that spot in 2019 before moving to the offensive line. Pihlstrom played in all eight games of the 2020 season, starting twice at left guard. He showed versatility, starting twice at right guard, twice at left guard and once as a sixth lineman in 12 appearances in 2021. Big Ten coaches voted Pihlstrom second-team all-conference for his play as a 13-game starter at center in 2022. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Former tight end who has added about 70 pounds to his frame during his career. He’s an average mover who lacks jolt getting into blocks but is consistent in latching in with his hands and finding his positioning. He knows how to play and has guard/center versatility, but he might lack the desired physicality and athletic ability for the next level.
strengths: Has two-position flexibility as center/guard. | Crisp, accurate two-hand underhooks into chest. | Slides hips into place for positioning at point of attack. | Good centering punch with right hand in protection. | Maintains even, steady base when mirroring. | Can arch back and brace hips to anchor.
weaknesses: No juice getting out of snap and into run fits. | Lacks pop into first contact. | Gets stood up and neutralized by big nose tackles. | Pulled forward and off-balance in pass pro. | Gap-to-gap quickness is below average versus delayed blitz.

bio: Ward was a long snapper at Choctawhatchee High School in Florida before joining UCF in 2017. He did not play in 2017 and 2018, redshirting his first year on campus. Ward took over the snapping duties for the next four years, making four tackles in 50 games for the Knights. He was a two-time finalist (2021, 2022) for the Patrick Mannelly Award, given to the nation's top long snapper. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ward returned for a sixth collegiate season to work on his frame and his game in 2022. He added muscle mass and looked a little more athletic in his final collegiate campaign. He’s fairly consistent as a short snapper, but his long snaps come out with average speed and spiral to the target. He has a chance to be a late-round pick but will find a camp invite if he doesn’t hear his name called in the draft.
strengths: Full-time snapper over the last four seasons. | Highly driven and highly intelligent. | Short snaps come out with good zip. | Improved consistency of short-snap placement in 2022.
weaknesses: Slow feet hurt pursuit and tackle potential on punts. | Below average velocity on deep snaps. | Deep snaps feature inconsistent spiral and placement.

bio: Gaye moved from Gambia, Africa's smallest mainland country, to the United States when he was 12 years old. He played at two junior colleges (Arizona Western College in 2018, Garden City Community College in 2019) after graduating from Edmonds-Woodway High School in Washington. He stood out immediately on a talented LSU defense in 2020, starting all 10 games and leading the Tigers with 9.5 tackles for loss to go along with two sacks, 32 tackles, one interception and six pass breakups. An upper-body injury limited Gaye to just four games in 2021 (19 tackles, 2.5 sacks), but he started 12 of 13 games played as a senior (36 tackles, six for loss with 2.5 sacks, two pass breakups, two forced fumbles). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Traits-based edge prospect who will need to improve his core strength and overall body control in order to allow those traits to make a difference as a pro. Gaye’s length and effort provide advantages at times, but tackles with power tend to give him an inordinate amount of trouble. He’s much more effective aligned wide of the tackle as a rusher and playing upfield or in gaps as a run defender. His tape shows flashes of rush potential, but finding the control and balance needed is a must.
strengths: Athletic frame with long limbs. | Uses length to separate from blockers. | Bend and stride length to slither past blockers. | Disruptive in a slanting front. | Decent hand usage at top of the rush. | Continues to play and pursue through whistle. | Consistently looking to pry open rush edges.
weaknesses: Plays with a high center of gravity. | Leggy and a little plodding in tight quarters. | Body control and contact balance are issues. | Kick-out blocks get him moved around. | Poor field awareness in locating the football. | Tackle’s punch disorients his rush. | Lacks pocket agility to finish sacks at off angles.

bio: McGhee made a good first impression at Kentucky Wesleyan in 2018, leading the team with six interceptions -- one returned for a touchdown -- as a true freshman (37 tackles, seven pass breakups in 10 games, seven starts). The Georgia product started 11 contests in 2019 (44 tackles, three for loss), tying for the team lead with three interceptions, and blocked a kick in each of his first two seasons. After playing in four games as a reserve in the spring of 2021 (10 tackles), McGhee moved on to Minnesota State, where he played in eight games with one start in the fall (17 tackles). Taking over the starting job for all 13 games in 2022, he garnered second-team All-Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference honors (63 tackles, seven for loss, two interceptions, eight pass breakups). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: McGhee will have to prove he can make the big jump in competition, but he has a coverage background at cornerback and at nickel. His ball production will be viewed favorably by teams. He has NFL size, adequate speed and was an impressive tester at his pro day. He could be a late-round pick or a priority free agent, but his play on special teams helps his chances of getting a look as a backup safety.
strengths: Adequate size, strength and speed. | Opportunistic player with 11 career interceptions. | Twitchy upper-body strength to toss blockers aside. | Uses short-area foot quickness to dart around blocks. | Has four career blocked kicks.
weaknesses: Needs to prove he can tougher competition in the run game. | Backpedal is a little tight and upright. | Lacks fluidity when swerving in space in zone coverage. | Gets crossed up by route fakes at break points.

bio: Jones signed with Tulane in 2018 after earning all-district honors as a dual-threat quarterback at Heritage High School in Frisco (1,834 rushing yards, 20 passing touchdowns as a junior). He became an excellent all-purpose player for the Green Wave, playing in all 13 games as a reserve his true freshman year (47-216-4.6, four TDs rushing; 6-52-8.7 receiving; 20-558-27.9 kick returns; 15-113-7.5 punt returns) before earning six starts in 2019 (61-371-6.1, four TDs rushing; 34-367-10.8, two TDs receiving; 34-732-21.5 kick returns; 11-141-12.8 punt returns in 13 games). Jones started twice in 10 appearances in 2020 (67-389-5.8, two TDs rushing; 14-101-7.2 receiving; 15-439-29.3 kick returns; 4-31-7.8 punt returns). He transferred to Georgia Southern for 2021, getting six starts in 10 games (41-196-4.8 rushing; 25-351-14.0 receiving), beginning one game at quarterback, one at running back and four at receiver. Jones started six of the first eight contests at receiver in 2022, setting career highs in receptions (35), receiving yards (483) and receiving scores (six) and returning kicks (12-112-9.3 punt returns; 1-16-16.0 kick returns) before falling to injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Slot receiver whose background with option football and as a returner could increase his chances with teams seeking versatility. Jones is a fluid athlete with the footwork to handle short to intermediate routes. He has natural hands but is likely to struggle dealing with tight man coverage and contested-catch situations that will come with it. Jones profiles as a zone-beating slot with the potential to return kicks.
strengths: Has option background as runner and quarterback. | Possesses solid top-end speed and foot quickness. | Potential to continue improvement as route runner. | Stems coverage out of the route path. | Above-average feel for space working against zone. | Quick hands to pluck throws outside his frame. | Extensive work as kick and punt returner.
weaknesses: Lacks play strength and aggression as 50/50 target. | Needs to improve catch-through-contact success rate. | Average competitiveness after the catch. | Too easy to bring down with the ball in his hands.

bio: Burney matriculated from St. Petersburg to Gainesville to play for the Gators in 2018. He played in 12 games as a reserve and on special teams that year (11 tackles, two for loss with one sack, two pass breakups). The cousin of NFL cornerback Brandon Facyson was a part-time starter the next three seasons, starting three of eight appearances in 2019 (37 tackles, one interception), four of 12 in 2020 (52 tackles, 2.5 for loss with two sacks, one interception, two pass breakups) and two of 13 in 2021 (44 tackles, one for loss, three pass breakups). Burney started all 13 games his final year with Florida, racking up career highs with 79 tackles, nine for loss with four sacks, two interceptions, four pass breakups and two forced fumbles. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Burney is an aggressive linebacker with a well-built frame and good play speed, but he lacks the instincts to play with consistency. He’s plenty fast and can beat blockers to the spot or chase down runners in the open field. He needs to work on his block take-on and might fit best as a weakside linebacker in a 4-3 defense. His ability to run with skill-position players in man coverage and potentially handle special teams reps help his cause.
strengths: Slices through creases and into playmaking position inside the box. | Good hustle laterally to beat climbing blocks to the spot. | Possesses speed to run with tight ends and running backs in coverage. | Soft hands with good ball skills. | Proactive tackler who takes away space from cutting runners.
weaknesses: Full-time starter for just a single season. | Needs better discipline and technique at the position. | Below-average instincts to make quick diagnosis. | Gets stuck to downhill blockers coming at him.

bio: Speed signed with Georgia as one of the top cornerback recruits in the country from Sandalwood High School in Jacksonville, Florida. He played in 11 games as a true freshman (five tackles) and then redshirted the following season (one tackle in two games). Speed played in a reserve role in 2019 (five tackles in 13 games) and 2020 (one tackle in nine contests) before finally getting three starts for the 2021 national champions (13 tackles in 13 appearances). He entered the transfer portal after the season, reuniting with former Georgia coach Mel Tucker at Michigan State. Speed started 11 of 12 games played in his final campaign, recording 62 stops and five pass breakups. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Speed’s tape and production don’t stand out. However, his rare size and speed, along with his potential to star on special teams, could give him a chance to find an NFL home.
strengths: Rare height/weight/speed combination. | Build-up speed to recover deep. | Size and strength to become a plus run defender. | Background and traits could make him a core special-teamer.
weaknesses: Very little ball production during his career. | Lacks sudden burst to stay connected at route breaks. | Below-average instincts and anticipation in coverage.

bio: Carlson joined the Tigers in 2017 but redshirted that season as his brother, Daniel, finished his All-American career as the SEC's all-time leading scorer before heading to the NFL. Anders did a solid job taking over his sibling’s duties in 2018 (15-25-60%; two-of-nine from 50-plus yards, long 53 FGs; 44-44 XPs) and in 2019 (18-25-72%, long 52 FGs; 48-49-98% XPs). He had his best year in 2020, receiving second-team All-SEC honors after tying for second nationally with 20 field goals made and tying for ninth-best in the FBS with a 90.9 percent field-goal make rate (24-25-96% XPs). His 2021 season was not as productive (14-21-66.7%, two blocked FGs, long 49; 35-36-97.2% XPs) and ended when Carlson tore the ACL in his left knee (non-kicking leg) trying to recover an onside kick against Mississippi State. He made 12 of 17 field-goal attempts (70.6%) and all 22 extra-point tries in 2022. Carlson was the team's kickoff specialist most of his career, kicking 183 touchbacks on 314 attempts (58.3%). He was also a three-time Academic All-American and selected to the Allstate AFCA Good Works Team. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Carlson has made kicks in big moments and appeared to be tracking in a good direction back in 2020. However, he has struggled to establish consistency on mid-range kicks and has been poor on kicks from 50 yards and beyond. He’s had too many kicks blocked during his career and doesn’t sport a booming leg on kickoffs.
strengths: Brother is an NFL kicker. | Possesses good size and has made kicks in high-pressure situations. | Was 4 of 4 from 40-plus yards in dramatic 2019 Iron Bowl win over Alabama.
weaknesses: Career make rate of just 71.8 percent. | Struggled to find consistent kickoff depth in 2022. | Made just 5 of 17 field goals from 50-plus yards, going 0 for 4 since 2021. | Highly inconsistent on mid-range kicks. | Slow operation time leads to blocked kicks.

bio: Carter's family moved to Missouri City, Texas, before his junior year of high school and he was a backup that season. He suffered a season-ending back injury his senior year. After one year at Cheshire Academy for prep school, he arrived at West Point weighing 225 pounds. Carter grew into a starting role in 2020, starting two of 10 appearances (14 tackles, one sack, one interception, one blocked kick). He made national headlines in 2021, ranking second in the FBS with a school-record 15.5 sacks and tying for 10th with four forced fumbles to go along with 44 tackles, 18.5 for loss, one interception, and two pass breakups in 13 starts. His production dropped as a senior, but he still led the team with seven tackles for loss (3.5 sacks) in 10 starts, missing two midseason games due to injury. The United States Military annual budget included language to prevent service academy athletes from deferring their mandatory post-graduation service, but the omnibus appropriations bill allowed certain service-academy athletes to continue requesting waivers from the Department of Defense. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Long and rangy, Carter is currently best suited as a 3-4 rush linebacker on passing downs, but is likely to develop into an every-down player with additional growth both physically and technically. Carter needs to play with more skilled hands and inject a little more glass into his on-field diet in order to meet force with force when the run game comes downhill at him. His explosive get-off and natural bend/agility at the top of the rush are enough to create early opportunities for himself as a quarterback hunter. Carter might need a longer runway to meet his potential, but if does his pass-rush homework, he could take a substantial leap forward as an odd or even front edge rusher by Year 3.
strengths: Finished 2021 season with 15.5 sacks. | Wingspan to excite evaluators looking for a future edge-setter. | Long frame with the potential to add substantial mass and muscle in the pros. | Explodes up the field to distress pass-setting tackles. | Long, bendy strides with the ability to flip his hips and cut corners of the rush arc. | Fairly effective rip-and-run mechanism with his rush. | Can make silky smooth transitions inside on two-way go. | Fluid feet for seamless inside spin counters.
weaknesses: Might need a redshirt year to hit weights and get bigger. | Can be a little too passive as a run defender. | Allows easy attacks into his frame by blockers. | Doesn’t play with much shock in his hands. | Doesn’t unglue quickly from punch once it lands. | Had issues dealing with additional attention from pass protection in 2022. | Drag-down tackler.

bio: Jones was a two-star recruit coming out of Varnado High School in Louisiana. He played in nine games in 2017 (nine tackles) and redshirted the following year (four tackles, one for loss in four games). Jones started nine of 14 appearances in 2019 (42 tackles, seven for Jones has unusual length and some interesting qualities as a player, but he remains a bit undeveloped in some respects and will need to flash in camp to rise above the practice squad. loss with two sacks) and then started all 11 of UL's contests in 2020 (43 tackles, 3.5 for loss with two sacks). Sun Belt coaches voted him third-team all-conference in 2021 as he posted 60 tackles, 9.5 for loss with six sacks, four pass breakups and two fumbles forced and recovered. Jones was a second-team pick as a senior, accumulating 51 tackles, 8.5 for loss including 7.5 sacks, in 12 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Long-limbed edge defender with an angular frame and a willingness to take on all comers. Jones’ production might not jump off the page, but he’s athletic and uses his length to put himself in position to make tackles. Jones could use more strength in his lower half both as a run defender and pass rusher. While they aren’t sustained, there are flashes of rush potential that might create a roster opportunity after a year on a practice squad.
strengths: Adequate size with good length along the edge. | Punches and separates from blocker before seeking out the ball-carrier. | Quick feet to dart around traffic looking for the tackle. | Attacks blockers with forceful hands and lead shoulder. | Decent three-step speed to the top of the rush arc. | Hits sudden inside stride to attack the B-gap. | Transitions from run defender to pass rusher quickly.
weaknesses: Somewhat lean in his lower half to maintain his base. | Fails to explode into blocker with enough force. | A little inconsistent with contain positioning. | Must become more threatening with his speed-to-power rush.

bio: Iosivas (pronounced yo-shee-vas) was a three-sport athlete (football, track, basketball) at Punahou School in Hawaii before matriculating to Princeton in 2018. He played in nine games as a reserve his redshirt freshman season (18-263-14.6, four TDs). The school did not play football in the fall of 2020 or spring of 2021 due to COVID-19 concerns. He earned second-team All-Ivy League honors in 2021 after leading the team with five touchdown receptions (41-703-17.1). He was a first-team all-conference selection in 2022 after leading the Tigers with 66 receptions for 943 yards (14.3) and seven scores in 10 starts. Iosivas competed with the track squad during his career with the Tigers, as well, including a fourth-place finish in the heptathlon at the 2021 NCAA Indoor Championships where he set an Ivy League record with 6,069 points in the seven events. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Iosivas’ size, speed and athletic ability might not overwhelm NFL opponents, but those traits do give him a very real chance of battling for an NFL roster spot. He needs to work on his catch technique and level up his aggression when competing for catch space, but his ability to become a three-level route runner should work in his favor.
strengths: Celebrated heptathlete with speed and leaping ability. | Runs with threatening lean into drive phase of the route. | Nifty foot quickness to beat press and elude tacklers. | Fairly sharp in stair-stepping coverage away from his pattern breaks. | Size and athletic talent to elevate and win downfield jump balls. | Quick transition from catch to run on zone-beater routes.
weaknesses: Has a tendency to pop upright into out-breaking routes. | Body catcher lacking natural ease with hands as pass catcher. | Looks labored when adjusting to throws outside his frame. | Allows defender too much leeway into catch space on bucket throws. | Not a very willful finisher in run-after-catch mode.

bio: Vorhees was an All-American offensive and defensive tackle at Kingsburg High School in California before joining the Trojans in January 2017. He played in 13 games as a true freshman, starting the final nine games at right guard. Vorhees started there again in 11 of 12 games played in 2018 despite having knee surgery after spring practices. He suffered an ankle injury the following year, redshirting after playing in two games as a reserve. Vorhees returned to the starting lineup five times in 2020, moving over to the left guard spot as 2021 first-round pick Alijah Vera-Tucker slid outside to tackle. He garnered third-team Associated Press All-American and honorable mention All-Pac-12 Conference honors in 2021, starting all 12 games (the first eight at left guard and the final four at left tackle). Vorhees was a first-team AP All-American and all-conference performer in 2022, starting 11 games at left guard (he missed three games due to injury). Unfortunately, Vorhees is feared to have suffered an ACL tear during his NFL Scouting Combine workout, per NFL Network Insider Tom Pelissero. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Guard prospect with five years of starting experience that shows itself with consistency and football IQ. Vorhees is a technically sound run blocker with a repeatable process. His range laterally and to the second level will be a little limited, but he’s an even-paced drive blocker, using excellent positioning, leveraged hands and churning legs. He needs to get quicker with inside hands in pass protection and guard against trying to protect his edges with his hands rather than a foot slide. The injury he suffered during his NFL Scouting Combine workout could cause him to fall in the draft, but he has the potential to become a starter when he’s fully healthy.
strengths: Five seasons of starting experience. | Steps into run fits at quality angles. | Consistently well-placed hands as drive blocker. | Leg churn bolsters block engagement and seal. | Reacts quickly to moving fronts post-snap. | Pass sets with a feel for A-gap pressure. | Passes off twisters cleanly to teammates. | Good firmness in outside hand to corral rusher.
weaknesses: More catcher than puncher, allowing some pocket push. | Needs to do a better job of sliding feet to constrict gaps. | Opponents can out-reach him with inside hands into his frame. | Very average climb quickness to second-level cutoffs. | Inconsistent securing first block back side on combos. | Blocks deteriorate into grappling matches at times.

bio: Orji starred at Rockwall High School in Texas before signing with Vanderbilt (where his older brother Alston played) for the 2019 season. He played nine games as a freshman (six tackles). Orji led the Commodores in tackles as a sophomore (66 tackles, 1.5 for loss, two pass breakups in nine starts) and junior (92 tackles, team-high 13 for loss with one sack in 12 starts). He again topped his squad with 108 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss (with two sacks) and three forced fumbles as a senior, starting all 12 games. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Orji plays a frenetic brand of football that helps get him to the football but also creates consistency issues. When the ball is snapped, he’s in attack mode whether he’s a run blitzer or an urgent linebacker. He makes up for what he lacks in timed speed with aggressive angles and an ability to slip climbing blocks to meet the ball-carrier near the line. He sees too many tackles slip from his grasp, but he’s also going to be in position to sniff a tackle when other linebackers are stuck to blocks. The traits, instincts and coverage are below average, but his play demeanor and special teams potential could give a chance to find a home.
strengths: Three-year starter and team captain. | Attacks with downhill flow to play ahead of linemen. | Stays square to the line with ready base when scraping. | Nice bend and lateral agility to slip around big bodies. | Plays active, urgent football. | Good feel for angles and timing as a blitzer. | Traits and demeanor to become a core special-teamer.
weaknesses: Inconsistent recognition of the blocking scheme. | Takes false steps and will get trapped behind blockers. | Needs to play with better control in pursuit of ball-carriers. | Below-average speed to range across the field. | Excessive missed tackle count over the last two years. | Average awareness and response quickness in zone coverage.

bio: Bradford was a four-star recruit in the 2019 class. He played in three games as a reserve during his redshirt season and suited up for seven contests off the bench and on special teams in 2020. Bradford started five of six games played in 2021 (one at right guard and four at left tackle) and missed eight games due to injury. He played in 13 games in 2022, starting 12 (11 at right guard, one at left tackle). He missed one contest, reportedly due to a coach’s decision. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Massive, scheme-specific guard prospect with plus power but obvious athletic limitations. Bradford has functional quickness as a pulling guard and can work from one block to the next with adequate timing. He can be effective as a single blocker but really shines on double teams, where he can help clear the pathway. His lack of lateral quickness and reactive athleticism can put him in a bind against one-gapping defensive tackles and sub-package rushers with short-area twitch. Bradford has the potential to become an eventual starter for gap and power teams.
strengths: Girthy and extremely wide in the gaps. | Size and strength are made for double-team blocking. | Plows run lanes open as an angle blocker. | On-field disposition can desirably sour against opponents. | Powerful hands can jar and cinch up defenders. | Snaps twisters across the gap with force. | Stands his ground against power rushers.
weaknesses: Lacks range, foot quickness and athleticism in protection. | Slow to slide and cut off inside moves. | Might be isolated and exploited by sub-package rushers. | Some inconsistency staying centered on run blocks. | Likely scheme-dependent in the run game.

bio: Cook started one game at cornerback for the Longhorns his true freshman season (18 tackles, one sack, one pass breakup), playing in all 14 contests. Cook started six of 11 appearances at corner in 2019 (24 tackles, one for loss, two pass breakups) and then played in all 10 games as a reserve the following season (18 tackles, 1.5 for loss). Coaches moved Cook to the Star position in 2021, where he started eight of 12 games played (46 tackles, three for loss with one sack, three pass breakups). He garnered honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference notice in 2022 (61 tackles, 3.5 for loss, five pass breakups in 13 games, 12 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Safety prospect with decent size and below average top-end speed. Cook has enough quickness to stay connected to routes, but he fails to play with the route recognition and instincts needed in coverage. He was a more consistent, physical tackler in 2021 and will need to get back to that style of play to give himself a chance to make a roster.
strengths: Possesses NFL-caliber size and length. | Showed explosiveness with above-average broad jump at pro day. | Ranges and challenges deep ball at the high point. | Adequate foot quickness for short-area movement. | Highly experienced on special teams.
weaknesses: Below average top-end speed. | Disappointing ball production, including no career interceptions. | Outflanked too often by wide-flowing run plays. | Mental mistakes as split safety led to touchdowns. | Fails to show anticipation for route breaks. | Too many arm-tackle attempts in 2022.

bio: Louisville signed Johnson as a four-star recruit from Chaminade-Madonna Prep in Florida. He started twice as a redshirt freshman in 2018 (14 tackles, two for loss, one interception, two pass breakups in 11 appearances) and three times the following year, when he tied for the team lead with three forced fumbles (also posting 27 tackles, two for loss, one interception and six pass breakups in 13 contests). Johnson played in eight games as a reserve in 2020 (two tackles, five pass breakups) before transferring to Virginia as a graduate student. He started 11 of 12 games played in 2021, tying for the team lead with three interceptions and recording 44 tackles, two for loss, and six pass breakups. Johnson was a first-team All-ACC pick in 2022, topping the squad with two interceptions, posting 51 tackles, three for loss, and 12 pass breakups in 10 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Johnson’s physical traits and natural footwork in phasing routes in space is very appealing, but certain athletic limitations could cause evaluators to pump the brakes when grading him. He can block a release from press or squeeze route breaks from his pedal or a side shuffle but will struggle to keep pace with deep targets from man. Sticky hips make flat-footed transitions and open-field tackling challenging tasks for him, so teams will need to have a plan for optimizing his strengths while minimizing his limitations.
strengths: Frame carries height, weight and length teams love. | Plays with above average play strength from press. | Finds his pacing and positioning as the route unfolds. | Surprising gather quickness in feet for a tall cornerback. | Excellent field balance defending high-low route concepts. | Odds of making a play on the ball tilt heavily in his favor when he’s in position. | Seven career interceptions, including five over the last two seasons. | Sheds blocks rapidly when attacking quick-game throws.
weaknesses: Lacks hip fluidity to open and flow with the release. | Mirror and match footwork is a little rough. | Allows immediate vertical separation when beaten off release. | Slow to change direction laterally and stay with route. | Can be too eager to jump short throws. | Not as physical or confident in run support as expected. | Limited agility creates tackling inconsistencies in open field.

bio: Johnson made an immediate impact as a three-star recruit from St. Petersburg, Florida, earning four starts for the Cyclones at cornerback as a true freshman (28 tackles, five pass breakups in 12 appearances). He garnered honorable mention All-Big 12 honors in 2019, tying for the team lead with 10 pass breakups and collecting 60 tackles, seven for loss with two sacks in 13 starts. Johnson received that honor from league coaches again in 2020 (40 tackles, two for loss, five pass breakups in 12 starts) and 2021 (55 tackles, three for loss, four pass breakups, two forced fumbles). He switched from corner to safety to lead the secondary in 2022, starting all 12 games (60 tackles, two interceptions, four pass breakups) to garner second-team all-conference recognition. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Cornerback turned safety with good athletic traits for the safety position and rare physicality from a former cornerback. Johnson has grown into a safety’s frame but is versatile enough to play near the line of scrimmage or line up over the slot. He moves fluidly with good play speed but is still processing angles and coverage responsibilities at his new position. He will come downhill and hit anything near the line of scrimmage with everything he’s got, but he needs to learn to control his aggression to become a more consistent tackler. Johnson’s traits, versatility and toughness give him a chance to become a starting safety or nickel safety.
strengths: Team captain with 54 career starts under his belt. | Sharp change of direction in the open field. | Rockets downhill to attack the run near the line. | Steps in and thumps blockers and runners. | Cornerback experience helps with route recognition. | Pedals and breaks with fluidity when matched over the slot. | Range to drive off the hash and challenge a boundary throw.
weaknesses: Still learning run fits and leverage as a safety. | Needs to throttle down and play with better control at times. | Run-support approach often creates an all-or-nothing scenario. | Has trouble gathering weight and making lateral tackles versus cuts. | Will take time learning responsibilities and recognition as split safety. | Inconsistent hips and leverage from near the hash.

bio: Richardson was one of the top quarterback recruits in the country coming out of Eastside High School in Gainesville (featured on the Netflix series "QB1: Beyond the Lights") despite suffering a season-ending injury his senior year. He played in four games as a reserve in 2020 (1-2, 27 yards, one TD, one INT passing; 7-61-8.7 rushing) and in eight contests with one start in 2021 (38-64-59.4%, 529 yards, six TDs, five INTs passing; 51-401-7.9, three TDs rushing), splitting time with Emory Jones, who transferred to Arizona State after the season. Richardson took over the starting job in 2022, throwing for 2,549 yards (176-327-53.8%, 17 TDs, nine INTs) and rushing for 654 yards and nine scores (103 carries, 6.3 per) in 12 games. Richardson opted out of the Las Vegas Bowl. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Dual-threat quarterback with an elite physical profile and a lot of work that needs to be done to reach a potentially high ceiling. Richardson’s frame, arm talent and mobility will demand respect as a potential first-round option. He has the ability to make plays on the move that very few of his NFL peers will be able to make. However, but his accuracy on short and simple throws left much to be desired due, in part, to shoddy footwork and inconsistent rhythm. The footwork issues can be corrected, but the challenge will be determining whether he can be at least a functionally accurate passer at the next level. Richardson’s potential to strike with the deep ball, attack the secondary from sideline to sideline and gash teams with his legs creates greater leeway in his projection as a developmental prospect. Ultimately, he will succeed or fail based on his ability to play with better post-snap recognition and deliver the football with consistency.
strengths: Elite size, strength and athletic ability for the quarterback position. | Has potential to perform in a variety of offensive schemes. | Can make explosive plays as a passer and runner. | Arm strength to throw downfield and into tight windows. | Functional pass accuracy when mechanically sound and in rhythm. | Willing to take a hit and still deliver the throw. | Good awareness of pressure mounting around him. | Footwork to slide and throw or scramble for yards. | Had touchdown-to-interception ratio of 12:2 over his final six games at Florida. | Ran for touchdowns of 45, 60, 73, 80 and 81 yards over the past two seasons.
weaknesses: Inconsistency and inaccuracy made it hard for him to have sustained success. | Could use a better feel for the timing of his progressions. | Needs to take some spice off short throws. | Below average touch and ball placement rolling out. | Hasn’t learned to manipulate coverage with his eyes. | Struggles to paint intermediate zone holes with anticipatory throws. | Accuracy issues are often a function of poor footwork. | Loses track of coverage and will throw into danger. | Too willing to flip the ball out instead of taking a sack.

bio: Green played in five games for the Tar Heels his true freshman season in 2018 (4-45-11.3), one year after leaving Florida's Rockledge High School as a four-star recruit. He started twice in 2019 (8-217-27.1, two TDs in 10 games) and once in 2020 (4-38-9.5, one TD in 11 contests) before grabbing the full-time spot in his fourth campaign (31-612-19.7, five TDs in 13 starts). Green was a third-team All-ACC selection in 2022 (43-798-18.6, seven TDs in nine games, eight starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Green’s size and deep-ball success make him a more intriguing Day 3 prospect than the overall production and skill set might suggest. Like most vertical specialists, he’s not going to shake man coverage on intermediate routes, but he has decent hands and consistently finds himself overtaking deep coverage with his build-up speed. He might find himself fighting for a spot on a practice squad or the back end of a roster.
strengths: Explosive athlete with sprinting and long-jump/triple-jump background. | Adequate lateral footwork to release and avoid the punch. | Vertical specialist who averaged 19 yards per catch at North Carolina. | Alters early route tempo to help surprise and create separation deep. | Confident and capable leaping and corralling the deep throw in mid-air. | Hands are typically reliable catching short and intermediate throws. | Deadens and drops feet in the field of play near the boundaries.
weaknesses: Ball-tracking on contested deep balls can be spotty. | Route transitions lack fluidity and acceleration at the turn. | Shortens his strides, giving away impending breaks. | Needs to battle for late catch space more consistently. | Build-up speed with average early acceleration. | Coverage can phase his intermediate routes.

bio: Harrison was a four-star recruit and was a top-200 prospect nationally for his play at Archbishop Carroll High School in Washington, D.C. He signed with Oklahoma for the 2020 season, playing in nine games as a reserve lineman his true freshman season. Harrison started 12 of 13 games played at left tackle as a sophomore in 2022 before starting 12 more contests in 2022 -- one at right tackle and the other 11 on the left side. The 2022 first-team All-Big 12 Conference selection opted out of the Cheez-It Bowl to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Collegiate left tackle with good size and length, but average athletic traits. Harrison is self-aware and does a nice job of utilizing his strengths to mask his weaknesses. He has a feel for pocket depth and uses his length and an inside-out approach to get the job done, but NFL speed could have him scrambling without help. Harrison lacks the pop and drive of a plus run blocker and is better at neutralizing opponents with proper positioning. There are some limitations athletically and it won’t always look fluid, but Harrison has the demeanor and football savvy to get the job done as a starter in time.
strengths: Hands remain punch-ready in protection. | Patient not to overset or overextend at the top of the rush. | Fires his hands with some pepper on them. | Finds full arm extension to maintain feel for rusher. | Will find work when uncovered. | Instinctive in his positional run blocking. | Adequate fluidity climbing to linebackers. | Activates hands to discard opponent’s punch.
weaknesses: Has trouble locating initial hands in run game. | Average foot chop with elevated pads as drive blocker. | Fails to knock opponents back at first contact. | Might not have slide quickness for desired diagonal sets. | Connection between feet and hands is disjointed. | Can be rocked backward by speed-to-power rush. | Below average agility to recover when beaten.

bio: Johnson appeared in seven games for the Aggies as a true freshman in 2020 (14 tackles, one pass breakup), starting at nickel back for the team's Orange Bowl win over North Carolina. The former four-star recruit from East St. Louis, Illinois, started all 12 games at that nickel spot in 2021, receiving the team's Defensive Playmaker Award (79 tackles, 8.5 for loss with one sack, one interception, five pass breakups). Johnson missed three games with an injury in 2022 but still was named first-team All-SEC after leading the team with three forced fumbles in nine starts (also posting 71 tackles, five for loss, one pass breakup). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Big, athletic safety with versatility to line up over the slot or inside the box for additional run support. Johnson has a strong passion for sticking his nose into whatever is going on near the line of scrimmage. He’s constantly flowing downhill to meet the play as close to the line of scrimmage as possible, but he needs to regulate his pace and angles to prevent overflowing and poor tackle balance. Johnson can be overmatched at the top of the route by top-end receivers, but he's capable of staying with pass-catching tight ends or a receiver with average speed. Johnson is positioned to become a good starter whose best ball will be played near the line of scrimmage.
strengths: Combines pro size with pro physicality. | Level of urgency should bolster any run defense. | Attacks blockers and dislodges quickly. | Puts every bit of his frame into ball-carrier when tackling. | Can play box safety or big nickel. | Able to line up over bigger targets in the slot. | Rapid response to both route breaks and quick game throws. | Transition acceleration keeps him close in man coverage. | Charges through pass-catcher to jar catch loose.
weaknesses: Not as consistent a tackler when playing deep. | Comes in hot and will overflow the target point. | Inconsistent coming to balance as an open-field tackler. | Backpedal is upright and lacking bend. | Allows too much cushion from off-man looks. | Cover talent diminishes the deeper he gets.

bio: Bush, a Cleveland native, redshirted the 2018 season but still played in four games, making three tackles and intercepting two passes against East Carolina and returning one for a score. The former first-team All-Ohio pick from Euclid High School missed the first four games of the 2019 campaign due to injury but returned to start five of 10 games played (19 tackles, six pass breakups). Bush started seven of nine games in 2020 (20 tackles, two for loss, two interceptions, three pass breakups) and 11 of 13 contests in 2021 (39 tackles, two for loss, three interceptions, six pass breakups) at nickel while Ahmad "Sauce" Gardner and 2021 Jim Thorpe Award winner Coby Bryant locked down the outside. Bush also blocked two kicks that season, which tied for second in the FBS. He was an honorable mention All-American Athletic Conference selection in 2022 as a 13-game starter (34 tackles, two interceptions, six pass breakups). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Outside cornerback with good size and above average footwork and recognition for pattern matching. Bush lacks top-end speed and plays off-man coverage to protect himself, but it allows for far too many catches underneath. He has twitchy, agile feet with the potential to squeeze the top of the route more effectively if given safety help. Bush’s instincts and ball skills give him a chance to be a middle-round pick as a zone or off-man corner.
strengths: Racked up 32 career passes defensed, including nine interceptions. | Stays low in his backpedal in ready position to pounce. | Smooth hips and feet to mirror route turns from off-man. | Recognizes routes and shades the breaks. | Plays with agile, sudden feet in transitions. | Plants and drives from pedal with almost no delay. | Scrappy getting off the perimeter blocks. | Blocked two field goals off the edge in 2021.
weaknesses: Plays way off receivers from off-man. | Declares and opens hips sooner than needed. | Allows excessive space for completions underneath. | Bites hard on double moves. | Lacks speed to stay with deep routes. | Loses proximity to coverage on multi-breaking routes.

bio: Green signed with Hutchinson Community College in 2018, intercepting six passes in eight games as a true freshman. Green was a top junior college recruit after his second year with the Blue Dragons, signing with Houston before the 2020 season. He played in eight games off the bench that year (10 tackles, two pass breakups). He played in all 14 games as a reserve in 2021 (19 tackles, one interception, two pass breakups) and then became a starter in 2022, posting 49 tackles, three for loss, with two interceptions and eight pass breakups to garner second-team All-American Athletic Conference accolades. Green was the Independence Bowl Defensive MVP (nine tackles, one pass breakup). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: As a cover man, Green is fairly patient and accurate in matching the release from press and can run with deep routes all day long. However, he struggles to stay connected to routes that feature change of direction. His run-support tape will work against him, too. Given his size, strength and athletic profile, a team could decide to take a chance on his traits late in the draft.
strengths: Quality size and strength as a press corner. | Blazed a 4.36-second 40-yard dash at his pro day. | Smooth feet match rhythm of the receiver's release. | Displays burst quickness on the throw from off-man. | Able to constrict catch space with frame and active hands.
weaknesses: Allows separation opportunities at break points. | Doesn’t utilize athletic gifts to his advantage often enough. | Too complacent in getting where he needs to go. | Lacks route recognition to play tight man. | Poor run defender.

bio: Richards was a three-star prospect who starred as a tight end and defensive end at The Haverford School in Pennsylvania before signing with North Carolina. He played in nine games as a reserve and on special teams in 2019 and then moved into the starting lineup for 11 of 12 appearances at left tackle as a sophomore. Richards started all 13 games at left tackle in 2021 and all 14 games at that spot in 2022 to garner third-team All-ACC accolades. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Richards is thick-hipped with good lower-body power fueling above average drive-blocking potential. He clears space when he’s centered into opponents, but he lacks the body control and hand consistency to do so on a regular basis. Pass protection concerns will be diminished with a move inside, but there will still be work needed when it comes to getting his feet in position to slow interior rushers. Richards’ drive blocking and potential position versatility give him a shot at a backup role with upside.
strengths: Three-year starter. | Well-developed lower half. | Understands where to target hand placement. | Carves out space with drive-blocking power. | Climbs his combo blocks with adequate timing. | Fires heavy hands into pass rusher. | Makes proper adjustments against twisting fronts. | Play strength benefits him in scramble situations in protection.
weaknesses: Below average body control. | Hasn’t learned to control and sustain his blocks. | Lacks athleticism to make all the blocks in space. | Heavy-legged getting around the corner when pulling. | Below average reactive athleticism in protection. | Fails to find proper footing to square up bull rushers. | Might not have slide quickness to protect outside edge.

bio: Mafi starred at Junipero Serra High School before signing with his home-state Bruins in 2018. He started nine of 12 games played as a freshman (17 tackles, two for loss). He started five games the next year (28 tackles, four for loss). He switched to the offensive line for 2020, playing in seven games as a reserve. Mafi started three of 12 appearances at right guard in 2021. He earned a second-team All-Pac-12 Conference nod for his play in 13 starts at left guard in 2022. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: With a wide frame that can be challenging to navigate for run defenders, Mafi plays with good core strength, a broad base and well-placed hands to improve his power zone. Move blocking in the ground game and reactive adjustments in pass protection will create difficulties for him due to a lack of foot quickness. He plays with a chippy temperament that coaches will like. Mafi is scheme-dependent, but he has the potential to be a good backup or low-end starter.
strengths: Built like a concrete block from shoulders to shoes. | Plays with a wide base and a broad power zone. | Able to generate pop in early stages of the block. | Good hand placement to fortify success as base blocker. | Throws a stiff punch to slow interior rushers in pass pro. | Chippy playing disposition shows up frequently.
weaknesses: Needs to guard against oversetting in pass protection. | Unable to muster recovery quickness to his back-side gap. | Lacks length and footwork to protect edges in space. | Will struggle getting to lateral angles as zone blocker. | Below-average connection rate to second-level linebackers. | Has trouble dropping pad level into leveraged positioning.

bio: Miller signed with Missouri as a four-star recruit, winning Tennessee Mr. Football Class 6A Lineman of the Year as a senior and leading Whitehaven High School to a state title. He played in 10 games as a reserve in 2017 (three tackles, missed three games with a leg injury) and 2018 (two tackles) and then redshirted the following year after suffering a season-ending knee injury in the opener. Miller played in one game in the fall of 2020 before deciding to opt out of the season and transfer to Jackson State, where he garnered first-team All-SWAC honors in the 2021 spring season (51 tackles, 4.5 for loss with 1.5 sacks in five starts). He was a first-team all-conference selection in the fall, as well, leading the Tigers with 109 tackles (11.5 for loss with 6.5 sacks, three pass breakups) in 13 starts. Miller starred in his final campaign, receiving second-team Associated Press FCS All-American and SWAC Defensive Player of the Year recognition by leading the Tigers with 117 tackles (11 for loss with 6.5 sacks) and five forced fumbles in 13 games (11 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Miller is patient but ready when keying the action and uses his anticipatory skills to help him stay cleaner than most undersized inside ‘backers. He aims to punish as a striker and is a capable open-field tackler when plays head outside the tackle box. He’s nothing special in coverage but displays the potential to become a plus special-teamer.
strengths: Vision and anticipation to shadow runner’s lane choices. | Slips blocks with squared pads and controlled lateral footwork. | Fearless to crash hard and punish downhill runners. | Plus agility and radar as an open-field finisher. | Impressive flashes in limited special-teams snaps. | Slides around traffic to find his target versus perimeter screens.
weaknesses: Needs to prove he can elevate his play versus better competition. | Plays with upright posture from the second level. | Struggles with punch timing to stack climbing blocks. | Lacks size to overcome mistakes in take-on positioning. | Inconsistent in coming to balance as downhill tackler. | Below-average stickiness in man coverage.

bio: Ajiake (pronounced AH-gee-kay) was a star running back at Bellarmine Prep in California before arriving in Las Vegas. He was a reserve defender and special-teamer in his first three seasons (five tackles in 10 games in 2018; 14 tackles in 12 games in 2019; seven tackles in six games in 2020). Ajiake was an honorable mention All-Mountain West Conference pick in 2021 (74 tackles), starting eight games before missing the end of the year due to injury. He garnered first-team all-conference honors in 2022, tying for ninth in the FBS with 132 tackles (11 for loss with four sacks) and intercepted two passes in 12 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ajiake lacks ideal size but he’s fast, explosive and agile. He’s often too passive in attacking the play, but when he’s proactive, good things often happen. He’s never going to be great at taking on blocks, so learning to flow downhill and slip blockers will be critical. He’s better suited in a chase-and-hit role as an outside linebacker in a 4-3 defense, but his pathway to a pro roster could be centered on his athletic profile and history as a productive special teams contributor.
strengths: Impressive explosion and short-area testing at pro day. | Pursuit burst and top-end speed to chase down the play. | Controlled and quick mirror-and-scrape from second level. | Athletic ability to find runners and finish plays behind or near the line. | Agility creates wider tackle range in the open field. | Starred on special teams coverage units earlier in his career.
weaknesses: Needs to balance the finesse with the physical. | Waits too long for the action to come to him. | Fails to challenge blocking schemes with proactive attack. | Slow to detach from second-level blockers. | Allows too many broken tackles due to a lack of tackle strength. | Delayed responder into coverage on play-action.

bio: Hearn began his collegiate career at Arizona, walking on there after starring as a two-time all-district pick at Oceanside High School in California. He started the final three games of his redshirt freshman season (26 tackles, one pass breakup in 12 games played) before transferring to Wyoming for 2019. Hearn started 10 of 13 appearances with the Cowboys (37 tackles, four pass breakups) that year and then started all six games in 2020 (13 tackles, four pass breakups) and all 13 games in 2021 (30 tackles, five pass breakups). Hearn returned to the Pac-12 for 2022, leading the Bruins with seven pass breakups in 13 games (six starts) while recording 40 tackles on the year. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: As a cornerback, Hearn does not offer the ball skills or anticipation necessary to handle zone or man duties in the NFL. However, as a safety, his size and athletic testing could create some interest from teams looking for him to make that position change. He’s a wrap-up tackler and does a nice job of taking on blocks. Hearn might be worth a peek for teams interested in developing him into a big nickel back or box safety.
strengths: Possesses physical talent and NFL measurables. | Size and toughness could help him make a move to safety. | Tools to potentially line up over slot tight ends. | Quick to punch and stuff perimeter blockers. | Plenty of experience tackling around the box.
weaknesses: Did not intercept a pass in 38 career starts. | Allows excessive space for offenses to play pitch-and-catch. | Too easily shaken at the top of the route. | Below-average reading and jumping the route. | Can be leggy in maneuvering as an open-field tackler.

bio: Potter was ranked among the nation’s top kicking prospects coming out of South Pointe High School in South Carolina. He made all seven extra-point tries and converted his only field-goal attempt as a college freshman (24 yards). Potter became the Tigers’ full-time placekicker in 2019 (13-21-61.9%, long 52 FGs; 79-79 XPs) and capped off the year with a 52-yard field against LSU in the national title game. He was an honorable mention All-ACC selection in 2020 after tying for sixth in the FBS with 18 made fields goals (18-23-78.3%, long 52 FGs; 61-62-98.4% XPs) -- although he had three kicks blocked during the season. Potter was a second-team all-conference pick in 2021 (21-26-80.8%, long 50 FGs; 38-38 XPs) and 2022 (20-26-76.9%, long 52 FGs; 49-49 XPs) and did not have any kicks blocked across 27 games those two seasons. He set school records for career field goals with 73 and for 50-plus yard FGs with nine. Also, he tied Clemson’s high-water mark for games played (69). Potter, who served as the team’s kickoff specialist since his freshman year, had a career touchback rate of 76.4 percent with 344 on 450 kicks. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Highly experienced kicker who holds multiple school and conference records. Potter generally hits kickoffs with good hang-time and distance for touchbacks. He has a gliding approach and strikes kicks with good consistency, but he has had some issues with mid-range reliability. While Potter has hit 9 of 13 from 50-plus during his career, he’s missed all four attempts from 55 yards and beyond.
strengths: Four years of kicking and five years of kickoff experience. | Banged 76.4 percent of his career kickoffs for touchbacks. | Strikes field goals with consistency. | Process is controlled and repeatable.
weaknesses: Made just 70 percent of his kicks from 30 to 49 yards during career. | Missed two field goals in the Orange Bowl loss to Tennessee. | Missed all four career tries from 55 yards or greater.

bio: BJ Ojulari is the brother of Azeez Ojulari, who starred as a pass rusher for Georgia before landing with the New York Giants as a second-round pick in 2021. BJ made his own name as a top national recruit out of Georgia's Marietta High School. He enrolled at LSU a semester early so he could play as a true freshman; he started once in 10 appearances in 2020 (16 tackles, five for loss with four sacks). Olujari led the Tigers with seven sacks among his 55 total stops, 11.5 for loss, in 13 games with 12 starts as a sophomore. He ascended to first-team All-SEC status in 2022, starting 11 games (58 tackles, 8.5 for loss with 5.5 sacks) and missing two early-season games with a knee injury. He opted out of the team's bowl game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Stand-up rush linebacker with upside as a pass rusher but inconsistent effort stopping the run. Ojulari is bendy as an edge rusher and will wreak substantially more pocket havoc once he builds a more complete rush plan. He plays contain as a run defender and has the pursuit speed to spill the run wide or make tackles in space, but needs to play with consistent effort on all run snaps. B.J. Ojulari possesses all the tools necessary to start for an NFL team once he adds a bit more polish to his game.
strengths: Brother, Azeez, was a second-round pick of the New York Giants in 2021. | Threatening get-off up the field. | Feet are coordinated and sudden on inside move. | Keeps feet charging forward through punch contact. | Uses ghost move (showing stab-move action before slipping inside arm away and dipping underneath) to defeat outside hand during rush. | Can dip the edge and flatten to the quarterback. | Strong secondary effort accompanies his counters. | Beats tackles and tight ends to contain positioning. | Stride and burst for pursuit success.
weaknesses: Needs to play with better toughness against the run. | Below average play strength for gap disruption. | Allows himself to be blocked too often. | Is a watcher when the ball isn’t coming his way. | Needs to keep pad level lower on inside move. | Hands a little lacking in activity and accuracy in his rush. | Just two sacks over his final eight games.

bio: Baylor inked Thompson out of England High School in Arkansas for the 2017 season, and he got one start in nine appearances for the Bears as a true freshman (three tackles, one for loss). He made an impact as a pass rusher in 2018 (15 tackles, 5.5 for loss with four sacks in 10 games, two starts) and on special teams, blocking three kicks. Thompson left the Bears before the 2019 campaign, however, sitting out that year and transferring to SFA. He topped the Lumberjacks with 8.5 tackles for loss and six sacks in 2020 (among 28 total tackles, intercepted one pass in 10 starts). Thompson was a first-team All-Western Athletic Conference pick in 2021, starting all 12 games (26 tackles, 12.5 for loss with 9.5 sacks, two pass breakups, two forced fumbles). He was a first-team pick again in 2022, his production waning but still tying for the team lead with five sacks among his 25 tackles, 6.5 for loss, and forcing a team-high three fumbles in 11 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Thompson will garner attention with his outstanding athletic testing, but there is still a lot of physical and skill development that needs to take place. He doesn’t have enough strength to set firm edges and is unable to generate speed to power as a rusher. His long strides can be an effective weapon as a rusher and when in pursuit, but he needs to crank up his intensity and get bigger to play in the league.
strengths: Big-time athletic tester with explosive hips and plus speed. | Stride length to get on top of protection quickly. | Possesses physical tools for molding as a rusher. | Uses agility, length and burst to finish in the pocket. | Speed to track down ball-carriers flowing wide.
weaknesses: Needs a year in an NFL strength-training program to get bigger. | Below-average strength and balance in lower half. | Not physical enough taking on the run. | Lacking a rush plan and a go-to counter inside. | Content to run up the field rather than attacking the play.

bio: Wilson was a tight end when he arrived at Quincy University in 2017 after playing at St. Louis University High School in Missouri. He grew into an offensive tackle during his redshirt season and earned starts in 10 of 11 contests the following fall, the first five games at right tackle and then the final five contests at left tackle. Wilson started 10 games at left tackle in 2019 and then started both of the team's spring 2021 contests on the blindside to garner first-team All-Great Lakes Valley Conference honors. He was a second-team all-conference selection in 2021, starting all 11 games, then ascended to first-team honors in 2022 as a nine-game starter at his left tackle spot. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A tackle prospect with NFL measurables, Wilson lacks the agility and short-area quickness needed to play outside as a pro. He dominated against inferior competition at times, but he failed to bulldoze opponents due his upright posture in the run game. He will need to become more limber to improve his pass slides and run-blocking consistency, but he faces an uphill battle to make a team even if he becomes a better performer in those areas.
strengths: Burly body type with thick chest and good length. | Engulfs linebackers with his mass. | Patient but firm latching in with his hands. | Displays ability to sustain as in-line blocker. | Mirrors inside rush moves with hands/feet synced.
weaknesses: Played against lower level of competition. | Pace of movement is gradual and lacks explosiveness. | Poor pad level creates below-average drive power. | Pass slides with a tight, narrow base, limiting speed to top of the arc. | Needs to prove he can withstand NFL speed-to-power rush.

bio: Sims caught seven touchdowns as a senior at Clark High School in San Antonio before heading north to play his college ball in Waco. He redshirted in 2018 (playing in three games with no receptions) before suiting up for eight games in 2019 (2-5-2.5 receiving), missing the end of the year due to injury. Sims bounced back to tie for the team lead with three touchdown catches in 2020 (14-164-11.7, six starts) and then garnered honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference honors as a junior (31-361-11.6, six TDs in 14 games, 13 starts) and senior (31-255-8.2, three TDs in 12 games, 11 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Tight end with average size and talent as a run blocker but the tools to get a little better in that area. Baylor frequently used Sims as a wingback who was asked to base block, lead block and get into space on outside zone. As a pass-catcher, he lacks separation talent and is going to get what is given to him by the defense. Sims’ average traits mean he will likely need to be in a favorable situation to make a roster.
strengths: Counted on to block in Baylor run game. | Patient fitting up into centered positioning as a run blocker. | Size, tools and willingness to become a more consistent blocker with work. | Confident hands-catcher. | Works the middle of the field and catches through contact. | Can deliver a heavy blow to tacklers during run after catch.
weaknesses: Slow to stop and settle into catch-ready positioning as a receiver. | Not much separation quickness and will wear man coverage. | Frequently late getting off the snap. | Brings helmet before hands as run blocker. | Needs to bring feet under him to prevent falling off the block.

bio: VanSumeren was named the Bay City Player of the Year as a senior at Garber High School after setting a state record with 85 receptions (1,259 yards, 13 TDs). He signed with the University of Michigan for 2018, playing in four games as a reserve fullback and on special teams during his redshirt season. VanSumeren played in five games in 2019 and then moved to linebacker for 2020 (seven tackles in six games with two starts). He transferred to Michigan State in 2021, playing in all 13 games with one start (12 tackles). He started 10 of 11 appearances as a senior (81 tackles, three for loss with two sacks, two pass breakups). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: VanSumeren’s production and game tape won’t draw draftable grades, but he possesses extremely rare athletic attributes for his position and that might create an opportunity with a team coveting elite traits. He’s not a thumper as a run defender and his football instincts leave much to be desired, but if he can prove himself as a special teams contributor in camp, he could force a team to give him a year on the practice squad for additional development.
strengths: Elite athletic testing results in line with what we typically see from receivers and cornerbacks. | Has experience as both a linebacker and fullback. | Plenty of scrape and pursuit quickness to chase the football. | Possesses athletic gifts to continue improving at his position. | Able to run with backs in man coverage.
weaknesses: Much better tester than player on tape. | Instincts are lacking. | Hasn’t learned to cause much mayhem with his athletic gifts. | Struggles to take on blocks and leverage his run fits. | Runs himself out of position in both phases. | Loses track of coverage duties, allowing easy catches.

bio: Williams signed with Illinois out of St. Francis High School in California. The three-star recruit started seven of 11 games played in 2017 (64 tackles, 1.5 for loss, three interceptions, two pass breakups). He was dismissed from the team in October 2018 for an undisclosed violation of team rules (playing in one game as a reserve with one tackle) and transferred to the College of San Mateo, where he was named a junior college All-American. Williams joined Oregon next, starting two of seven appearances in 2020 (15 tackles, two for loss, two pass breakups). He started three of five games played in 2021 (21 tackles, two for loss), intercepting three passes and returning one for a score despite missing nine games with a broken fibula. Williams stayed on the field for 13 starts in 2022, garnering honorable mention All-Pac-12 Conference accolades by leading the Ducks with 72 tackles (1.5 for loss with one sack), intercepting two passes, breaking up six other passes and forcing two fumbles. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: If Williams were 20 pounds heavier, he would be in consideration for a linebacker role in the NFL thanks to his nose for the football and style of play. He’s at his best near the line of scrimmage and playing the run, but his athletic deficiencies are hard to ignore as it pertains to his ability to hold up in coverage at the next level. Williams needs a very specific role as a box safety and will need to prove he can be a star on special teams.
strengths: Throws hands with pop to greet blockers with force. | Wide-eyed tackler who sees what he hits. | Plays with a blend of urgency and physicality in the box. | Opportunistic, finishing career with eight interceptions. | Potential to compete for core special teams duties.
weaknesses: Below average top-end speed will be a concern. | Hips are tight on his flip-and-run. | Lacks open-field agility to squeeze windows from zone. | Can be mismatched and exploited downfield in man coverage. | Has trouble getting free from a block.

bio: Robinson was twice named the top high school football player in Arizona, ranking as one of the top recruits in the country after putting up three 2,000-yard seasons. Texas won the battle to secure his services for 2020 and he came through as a true freshman, leading the Longhorns with 703 rushing yards. He broke the school record, averaging 8.2 yards on 86 carries (15-196-13.1, two TDs receiving). Robinson started 10 games in 2021, garnering first-team All-Big 12 honors by again leading Texas with 1,127 yards and 11 scores on the ground and ranking eighth in the FBS with 142.2 all-purpose yards per game. His final season in Austin was memorable, as he won the Doak Walker Award as the nation's top running back. Robinson was also a first-team Associated Press All-American and All-Big 12 selection after ranking sixth in the FBS with 1,580 rushing yards (258 carries, 6.1 per) and tying for fifth with 18 rushing touchdowns (19-314-16.5, two TDs receiving) in 12 starts. Robinson opted out of the Alamo Bowl. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Full-menu back blending a smorgasbord of position-specific traits that allow him to affect games. Robinson is well-built with a compact lower half and pairs a low center of gravity with agile feet. There are elements of both fight and flight in his running style, but defenders can never be quite sure what they are going to get.
