His ball skills and feel for positioning on deep throws and jump balls are unquestioned. Limiting his focus drops on short and intermediate throws will be critical to becoming a long-term NFL contributor.
strengths: Highly competitive against bigger/stronger Ohio State corners in 2022. | Accelerates to his top speed in a hurry. | Keeps routes moving at an elevated tempo. | Good ball skills to track and time the deep throw. | Clever hands and positioning help carve out catch space. | Makes winning plays on back-shoulder throws. | Can be elusive when needed after the catch. | Has three career punt return touchdowns.
weaknesses: High percentage of career catch tries were contested. | Quicker than fast with average deep separation. | Hip tightness limits in-and-out quickness at route breaks. | Doesn’t always finish his routes. | Loses catch focus working into the middle of the field.

bio: The first-team All-State pick at Germantown High School started seven of 13 games played in 2019 (19 tackles, one interception, three pass breakups) after playing in all 12 games as a reserve his true freshman campaign (22 tackles, one sack, one interception, two pass breakups). He was a second-team All-Big Ten selection in 2020 after he posted four interceptions (along with 30 tackles, two for loss, one pass breakup). Williams led the team with 11 pass breakups the following fall, recording 41 tackles and starting nine of 11 games played. He completed his college career in 2022 (40 tackles, 2.5 for loss, seven pass breakups in 10 starts), missing two games with a shoulder injury. Williams wears jersey No. 23 to honor a youth football teammate who passed away from leukemia. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Williams lacks the length and explosiveness of an outside corner but displayed his play strength and toughness at that position in the Big Ten. Williams has decent mirror-and-match footwork from press but can be a little late to accelerate quickly when forced to flip and chase. He plays with good recognition from zone and is quick to dart in on throws. His physical/athletic profile does not stand out and the lack of takeaways over the last two seasons could hurt him.
strengths: Plays with the footwork to shadow comeback routes. | Adequate stop-start to phase the double move. | Quick response to the quarterback's actions in zone. | Attacks throws on the catch side of receivers. | Fires downhill ahead of blocking wideouts to challenge ball-carrier.
weaknesses: Lacks height and length to play on the perimeter. | Failed to grab an interception over the last two seasons. | Inconsistent adherence to proper leverage against the route. | Gives away too much space to receivers near the goal line. | Rarely locates the football once his back is to the throw.

bio: Jones was a four-star recruit from Steele High School in Texas, where he was the District Defensive MVP as a senior. He jumped into the starting lineup for the Aggies as a true freshman, leading the team with six pass breakups in 10 games (30 tackles, one interception). Jones started all 12 games in 2021, posting 35 stops, two interceptions and six more pass breakups. In May 2022, Jones held a football camp for kids at Fort Hood to honor military families; his parents both served in the Navy and his mother now works at Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio. Jones started 10 games in the fall (33 tackles, two pass breakups), missing two contests due to injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Big, long cornerback with imposing size but a lack of functional footwork and route anticipation to stay connected to NFL route runners. Jones can be lackadaisical with his technique, so improving in that area could play a big role in bolstering his coverage consistency. He might lack the long speed for foot races in press-man work so Cover 2 and Cover 3 could be his coverage destination thanks to his size and potential physicality, but a move to safety should not be out of the question.
strengths: Three-year starter. | Premium size and length. | Big but fluid in his hip swivel. | Able to hog the catch space when contesting. | Takes quality closing angles on the throw. | Fights through receiver to break up passes. | Quick to trigger and wrap up versus quick game throws.
weaknesses: Technique is loose and undisciplined. | Too easily routed out of position. | Gives up instant separation at break points. | Below average long speed as a cornerback. | Struggles to stay in phase with comeback routes. | Left reaching and recovering in off-man. | Loses his leverage as run supporter.

bio: School with 1,941 rushing yards and 32 scores, then logged 11 games as a true freshman with the Vols in 2018 (52-185-3.6, three TDs rushing; 1-10-10.0 receiving). He practiced at linebacker in 2018 and moved to defense permanently in the fall of 2019. Banks was dismissed from the team on Oct. 4, 2019, after four games. Then-Tennessee head coach Jeremy Pruitt made the move after two separate off-field issues came to light. First, video was made public on Oct. 1 of Banks being arrested following a traffic stop on Sept. 15, when police discovered he had an outstanding warrant for failure to appear in court on a charge of driving with a suspended license. In the video, Banks makes highly charged and derogatory comments to police. Banks issued an apology after the video was released, stating he was “embarrassed by my actions that night.” On Oct. 4, the day Banks was dismissed from the team, TMZ published a video of an Aug. 24 incident, during which a woman alleges Banks had harassed her for months and had threatened her. Banks returned to the team in the fall of 2020, playing in nine games as a reserve. Banks became a top defender in 2021, leading the Vols with 128 tackles and tying for the team lead with 11.5 tackles for loss with 5.5 sacks (also intercepting a pass and breaking up three others with 13 games, 11 starts). He started eight of 11 contests played in 2022 (53 tackles, 4.5 for loss, four pass breakups), opting out of the Orange Bowl to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Inside linebacker who makes up for being slightly undersized with physicality. Banks' instincts and recognition improved in 2022, but he can still get better in those areas. He plays with below-average short-area twitch and just modest pursuit speed from sideline to sideline but will hit and wrap what is in front of him. He’s a likely two-down backup who might come off the field on passing downs but run back out for special teams reps.
strengths: Showed improvement in play recognition in 2022. | Scrapes along the front with squared pads. | Solid technique to play off of or around the blocker. | Adequate feel for efficient track to the runner between the tackles. | Will fly into the gap to meet runner where he lives. | Widens out and wraps to tackle with bear-hugging arms.
weaknesses: Athletic frame is a little light for an inside linebacker. | Lateral pursuit slides lack suddenness to avoid blocks. | Inconsistent feel for leveraging his gaps. | Loses ground to the runner when play flows wide. | Lacks certainty with his coverage duties. | Documented off-the-field issues while at Tennessee.

bio: Cooper was a three-star prospect out of Mount Carmel High School in Illinois. He played in four games as a reserve while redshirting his first year with the Bearcats in 2018. He started the first four games of the 2019 season at left guard before suffering a season-ending injury against Marshall. Cooper played in nine games with starts in the first three contests in 2020 before starting all 14 games at left guard during Cincinnati's run to the College Football Playoff in 2021. He started the first eight games of the 2022 campaign at left guard, playing in 12 games overall. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Cooper has extremely long arms for his height and he does a nice job of getting the most out of his physical ability. While his short-area athletic testing was average, he appears to be much quicker on tape and has the ability to make blocks on the move, although sustaining them is a problem for him. He’s solid in pass protection and plays with decisiveness that bolsters his consistency against gaming fronts. Cooper’s guard-only designation could hurt his chances, but he has the talent to compete for a spot on a roster.
strengths: Tremendous length with a wingspan of close to seven feet. | Gets around the edge with good athleticism on pull blocks. | Shows ability to make sudden adjustments to moving targets. | Maintains proper base width as a drive blocker. | Good recovery and hand resets in pass protection. | Athletic feet for competitive mirroring against quickness.
weaknesses: Fails to latch in and sustain for long. | Has trouble keeping run blocks in his power zone. | Hands can get too wide when making second-level contact. | Leans over his feet at times when punching rushers.

bio: Carvin was born in Guam, as his mother, Shonda Thomas, served in the Navy. The family eventually moved to Memphis, where he earned all-region honors as a senior at Cordova High School. The four-star recruit started six games (five at right guard, one at left guard) in 12 contests played as a freshman. Carvin started the final seven games at right guard in 2019, playing in 12 games. He started four of 10 games played at right guard in 2020. He started all 13 games in his fourth season with the Vols (seven at left guard, five at center, one at right guard) as well as in his fifth (all at left guard). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Carvin doesn’t display much displacement power when he’s getting into drive blocks, but he does flash enough movement to work in a variety of blocking schemes. His slide quickness is just average, but he does mind his protection gaps with solid body control. His hands are accurate and quick when he punches. His ability to play all three interior positions could give him a leg up if he’s in a camp battle, but his upside is limited.
strengths: Team captain with 43 career starts. | Adjusts and runs gap-shooters out of the way. | Offers potential to play in a variety of run-blocking schemes. | Pass punch is efficient and thrown with good timing. | Has the anchor to slow down bull-rushing tactics.
weaknesses: Doesn’t have the bend to aid with block sustain. | Needs to play with better balance blocking on the move. | Doesn’t get much pop as a down-blocker. | Could struggle recovering effectively to back-side gaps in protection.

bio: Reed picked off seven passes as a senior at Olive Branch High School, then intercepted two more passes for Northwest Mississippi Community College as a true freshman in 2018. He transferred to New Mexico after that season, starting 10 games for the Lobos (51 tackles, three for loss, one interception that he returned for a score). Reed intercepted four passes in seven games (five starts) in 2020, also posting 33 tackles and three pass breakups to garner first-team All-Mountain West Conference honors. Reed was an honorable mention All-MWC selection his final two seasons, starting all 12 games in 2021 (team-high 89 tackles with one interception and seven pass breakups) and 2022 (94 tackles, 4.5 for loss, one interception, 11 pass breakups, two forced fumbles). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A productive safety with above-average football smarts, Reed might need to make a permanent move to a nickel role with backup safety roster flexibility. He covers with good footwork and is patient not to commit his hips prematurely against fakes. He works to squeeze tight to his targets through the route but could have issues against leapers who can go over the top of him. He’s a willing run supporter but the stopping power falls a little below the mark. He will have some work to do to find a full-time home in the league.
strengths: Plays with good awareness and a high football IQ. | Four-year starter with above-average ball production. | Plus route reader with aggressive swipes at catch point. | Good awareness against play-action and rub routes near goal line. | Has a feel for the route and the quarterback’s eyes. | Patient when mirroring routes and rarely falls for fakes.
weaknesses: Below average height/length to play safety in the NFL. | Big runners can barrel past him in open-field tackle situations. | Overestimates his pursuit speed and ends up with suspect angles. | Will need to play less handsy in coverage. | Teams can target him on jump balls.

bio: Clark had 26 receiving touchdowns and 31 sacks during his career at Brighton High School in Massachusetts. He redshirted in 2018 and then moved from tight end to defensive tackle in the spring of 2019. Clark missed the fall due to injury but returned to start 11 of 12 appearances in 2020 (31 tackles, four for loss with two sacks) and 11 of 13 contests played in 2021 (33 tackles, four for loss with two sacks, two pass breakups). He used his massive frame to collect third-team All-Sun Belt plaudits as a senior (41 tackles, 10 for loss with 3.5 sacks, one blocked kick). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Nose tackle whose size is a double-edged sword. Clark lacks the build and body type of a true NFL nose, so additional weight limits his natural athleticism inside. He needs to make better use of his length to begin stacking blocks and controlling the point of attack. Clark is a former high school tight end with decent feet, so improved quickness could help him become a more disruptive interior talent.
strengths: Team captain who possesses a 6-foot-10 wingspan. | Adequate foot quickness for his size. | Gets off the ball and into the block with force. | Decent strength to challenge double teams. | Could become more disruptive at lighter weight.
weaknesses: Lacks desired lower-body thickness for a nose tackle. | Fails to play with consistent hand skill at take-on. | Ends up on the ground too often. | Below-average knee bend to sink and leverage. | Allows punch to linger on his frame rather than dislodging it.

bio: Cage played sparingly as a redshirt freshman in 2018 (one tackle in three games) and in 2019 (four tackles, one for loss) behind the Buckeyes' talented depth on the interior. Cage got his first collegiate start in the team's national championship game appearance at the end of the 2020 season. He played in seven games overall, making five tackles on the year. Cage started three times in 2021, making 11 appearances in total (10 tackles, four for loss with one sack). Cage started three of 12 appearances in 2022 (12 tackles, 2.5 for loss with 1.5 sacks). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Interior defender with average size, good length and below-average tape. The Ohio State scheme didn’t ask Cage to make many plays, but he might not have had the play strength or talent to do so if needed. He has decent feet and plays with effort through the snap, but it appears he won’t be able to control blockers or threaten the pocket often enough to make it as a pro.
strengths: Above-average wingspan. | Adequate first-step quickness off the snap. | Uses slap and arm-over to slip past the edge. | Footwork to work under and around a seal block. | Decent reactive quickness in working off the block.
weaknesses: Minimal production during his time at Ohio State. | Made just seven career starts. | Unable to muddy the interior as a block neutralizer. | Struggles to constrict his gaps when facing power. | Allows centers to play under his pads too often.

bio: Ji'Ayir (pronounced jye-YEAR) "Tig" Brown gained his nickname because he loved to bounce as a toddler, just like Tigger from the "Winnie the Pooh" books. He garnered first-team all-state honors as a senior at Trenton Central High School. From there, he enrolled at Lackawanna College, where he played with future Penn State teammate Jaquan Brisker and earned first-team All-American honors his sophomore year. Brown played in nine games as a reserve in 2020 (six tackles, one for loss, one pass breakup) before breaking out in 2021 playing next to Brisker. He was a third-team All-Big Ten Conference pick, tying for the FBS lead with six interceptions, posting 73 tackles and breaking up five passes in 13 starts. Brown was the team's Most Valuable Player in 2022, garnering third-team All-Big Ten Conference accolades with a team-high 74 tackles (seven for loss with 4.5 sacks) and four interceptions while also breaking up three passes and forcing two fumbles in 13 starts. He was the Defensive MVP of the Rose Bowl (eight tackles, 1.5 sacks, interception) in Penn State's win over Utah. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Versatile defensive back who has shown the ability to line up over the slot, play as a down safety and patrol the outfield as a Cover 1 safety ready to read and range. The lack of speed and explosiveness Brown showed at the NFL Scouting Combine won’t help his draft stock, but he’s a fiery run defender and plays with undeniable coverage instincts. He has an excellent motor that fuels him throughout the game, as well. He needs to play with a little more discipline or veteran quarterbacks and play-callers will bait him into mistakes. Brown’s versatility and football character could help him eventually become an NFL starter.
strengths: Brings energy, leadership and passion to his team. | Plays with the same motor throughout the game. | Versatility as nickel corner or safety. | Rapid diagnosis of quarterback’s intentions. | Triggers downhill into the catch point. | Nabbed 10 interceptions over two seasons as a starter. | Good closing burst in coverage, as a blitzer and as a tackler. | Determined and physical as a run supporter.
weaknesses: Can be frenetic and inefficient with his movement. | Desire to make plays can be used against him. | Moved out of position by quarterback’s misdirection. | Needs to maintain an expanded field focus. | Inconsistent matching route breaks effectively. | Must play with better downhill control and positioning as a tackler.

bio: Wisconsin grabbed the Indiana Mr. Football Offensive Lineman out of Bishop Dwenger High School. He played in two games as a redshirt freshman in 2020 before taking the reins of the offense in 2021, starting 11 of 12 games played at center to garner honorable mention All-Big Ten Conference recognition. Big Ten coaches voted him honorable mention again in 2022, as he started 12 games in the pivot before opting out of the team's bowl game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Two-year starter with the weight room strength and athleticism for work in a variety of run schemes. Tippmann is taller than your average center, but he can bend enough to neutralize at the point of attack. He’s a fluid move blocker who can make wide pulls, climbing cut-offs and adjustments to moving targets in space. He’s recognized for his football intelligence in the pivot and is an effective communicator. He needs to play with better posture and tighter hands to stay mirrored in protection and to improve his body control through engagement. Tippmann’s size, strength, smarts and athleticism should help him become a starter in the NFL.
strengths: Proportional thickness with strength to neutralize. | High football IQ with ability to make calls and adjustments. | Unlocks hips and rolls them into blocks. | Plus athlete who can zone block, pull or climb with relative ease. | Fluid with reactive athleticism to adjust to targets in space. | Flexible lower body allows him to cast solid protection anchor. | Keeps head on a swivel to spy and protect both A-gaps. | Dumps blitzers on the ground with upper body power.
weaknesses: Off-balance when playing too far forward off the snap. | Must make concerted effort to keep pad level low. | Average balance and body control through sustain phase. | Leads with helmet/pads, leaving frame open to defenders’ hands. | Lacks leverage to generate drive movement at the point. | Needs to play with flatter back and inside hands. | Leaning slows lateral transitions to mirror incoming twists.

bio: Wilson was a high school quarterback who transitioned to tight end at Central Michigan. He played in four games (1-5-5.0) during his redshirt season and then started one of three games played in 2019 (1-7-7.0). Wilson entered the starting lineup in three of five appearances in 2020 (5-50-10.0) before stepping into a leading role on offense the next fall (31-367-11.8, six TDs in 13 games, 11 starts). He topped the Chippewas with six receiving scores as a senior (44-445-10.1 in nine starts) despite missing the end of the year with an ankle injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Wilson doesn’t have the play strength or technique of a Y tight end and might not have the speed to threaten the seam as a pass-catching option, but it is still easy to like his game. He’s clever as a route-runner and shows an ability to create separation with decent success underneath, but he must become even more competitive on contested catches. Wilson’s run blocking needs work, but he’s willing and will have potential in that area if he can get much stronger.
strengths: Creative route-runner with good tempo variance. | Gets in and out of breaks with subtle stutter-step. | Makes instant transition from catch to run for additional yardage. | Handled pass protection and blitz pickup.
weaknesses: Below-average body control fitting into move blocks. | Doesn’t have the core strength to sustain base blocks. | Needs to fight harder for positioning on contested catches. | Gets delayed by pressure on release. | Average catch radius and jump-ball talent.

bio: Fisher was a two-time all-Maryland defensive end at Clear Spring High School and the team's top offensive lineman for four seasons before he committed to his home-state Terrapins. Coaching turnover there led to a transfer to Towson but he eventually went back home to work for his father, a locksmith. He signed with Shepherd for 2017, redshirting at tight end that year and then not playing in 2018. He gained enough weight to start all 13 games at right tackle in 2019, receiving second-team All-Pennsylvania State Athletic Conference East honors. The Rams did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns and Fisher did not play in the team's lone game in the spring of 2021. He started all 15 games at right tackle in 2021, however, garnering the first of two straight first-team All-PSAC East accolades. Protecting record-setting quarterback Tyson Bagent again for all 15 games in 2022, Fisher was named a first-team Associated Press Division II All-American. His brother, Dustin plays tight end and fullback at Shepherd. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Three-year starter and team captain with NFL size, toughness and athletic qualities. Fisher bullied his level of competition on a regular basis. He’s thick and powerful with the clinch strength and balance to sustain blocks through contact, but a move up in competition will surely test him right out of the gate. Fisher plays with more advanced elements of pass protection than is typical of his level of competition. His lateral quickness and athleticism should have him set as a move blocker and when mirroring athletic rushers in protection. Fisher has the traits and talent to slide from tackle to guard and become a solid NFL starter.
strengths: Team captain with tough field demeanor. | Broad frame with NFL thickness in upper and lower body. | Fits into blocks with forceful double underhooks. | Power to torque opponents off-balance. | Athletic and nimble enough to make reach blocks and mirror in protection. | Hand and core strength to sustain through movement. | Works to reset hands when he’s behind on positioning. | Efficient to snap and receive against twisting rushers.
weaknesses: Has played against a lower level of competition. | Must prove he can handle NFL size and strength. | Needs to reduce usage of outside hands on the move. | Pass rushers can get into him first due to his punch preference. | His aggression must be balanced out with technique. | Inconsistent timing on second-level strikes.

bio: The son of former Steelers star Joey Porter was a first-team all-state pick at North Allegheny High School before appearing in four games in 2019 (three tackles, one pass breakup) and taking a redshirt. He garnered honorable mention All-Big Ten honors in 2020, starting eight games (33 tackles, two for loss, four pass breakups). Porter was a third-team all-conference pick in 2021, starting all 13 games (51 tackles, one interception, four pass breakups). He vaulted to second-team Associated Press All-American and first-team all-conference status in 2022, also winning the team's Most Valuable Defensive Player Award (27 tackles, 11 pass breakups in 10 starts) despite missing two late-season games with appendicitis. He opted out of the Rose Bowl. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ascending cornerback combining traits and above average play strength that create a clear definition of who he is as a player. He can reroute the release and has the frame to close catch windows against big receivers in press-man or Cover 2 looks. Delayed transitions and sluggish change of direction put him in conflict in off coverages, so teams must pay attention to matchups and scheme in order to avoid a field full of yellow laundry. There is work to be done to improve tackle consistency in the run game, but he finishes tackles after a catch. Porter has scheme limitations, but he also has CB1 potential with more work and if utilized properly.
strengths: Father is a former Pro Bowler and was an undisputed alpha during his playing career. | The most physical reroutes in this year’s draft. | Smart hand usage helps cover when feet are late. | Recovery and length to swat away would-be catches underneath. | Closes the catch space when he’s in position. | Can win high-point challenges even from trail position. | Matchup potential against pass-catching tight ends. | Spins sticky tackle web when he gets his hands on receivers.
weaknesses: Noticeable delay in transitions from press. | Struggles to slide and match release quickness. | Not twitchy enough to match a complex route. | Too grabby at the top of the route. | Needs extra steps to plant and drive from top of his drop. | Lacking change-of-direction quickness as open-field tackler.

bio: Minnesota brought in Schmitz as a three-star recruit and top-10 center prospect nationally out of Homewood-Flossmoor High School in Illinois. He played in 13 games as a reserve his redshirt freshman campaign, then started four of 13 games played at center the following year. Schmitz started six games in 2020, earning honorable mention All-Big Ten honors from league coaches for his efforts. He was a second-team All-Big Ten Conference pick in 2021 as a 13-game starter for the Gophers. Schmitz returned for a sixth season in 2022, garnering first-team Associated Press All-American and all-conference honors for his play in 12 starts. He opted out of the team's bowl game. Schmitz was a second-team Academic All-American selection in 2022. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Schmitz is a highly consistent zone-scheme center with decent size. He is well-schooled in all phases of the run game. He consistently uses the proper footwork and angles to find early positioning and has the tenacity to finish blocks at a high rate. He has plus football intelligence and makes the calls for his offense. His drive power is average and he can be hit-or-miss getting to second-level targets. Schmitz lacks length and his edges will get a little leaky in pass protection from time to time, but his overall technique and teamwork in the run game should create a plug-and-play opportunity in the pros.
strengths: Makes all the calls up front. | Lateral quickness for reach blocks in outside zone. | Patient to find lateral positioning before engaging the block. | Captures defender’s edge with firm outside hand. | Plays with outstanding teamwork inside his scheme. | Consistent as a block finisher. | Maintains proper balance to pass and receive twists. | Able to unlock hips and ankles to drop a sudden anchor.
weaknesses: Below average adjustments to moving targets. | Can improve his timing when working up to his second block. | Arm length is below average. | Gets overextended with aggressive pass-setting slides. | Allows his edges to become too leaky when his edge is attacked.

bio: Ojukwu starred at Boise High School, lettering in wrestling and track and garnering first-team All-Idaho notice on the gridiron as a senior. As a redshirt freshman, he started the final seven games of the year at right tackle for the Broncos, playing in 12 games overall. Ojukwu started 11 games on the right side in 2019 before switching to left tackle the next year. He was named second-team All-Mountain West Conference that season and a first-teamer in 2021 after starting all 12 games on the blindside. Ojukwu was a first-team pick in 2022, as well, starting all 14 games at left tackle. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: College tackle with the build and skill set that would make him a better fit at guard in the NFL. Ojukwu has played a tremendous amount of college football and has a solid understanding of fundamentals. He uses big hands and long arms to jar and displace opponents at the point of attack, but it can break down quickly for him when he’s forced to operate in space as a run blocker or in pass protection. Ojukwu’s athletic limitations are balanced out by his size and power. He should compete for a roster spot as a late Day 3 selection.
strengths: Made 51 career starts at Boise State. | Tremendous personal character and coachability. | Excellent blend of size, length and strength. | Power in upper body to displace opponents. | Fits up run blocks and drives from in-steps with wide base. | Better inside hands will instantly improve protection consistency. | Size to squeeze down and block off A- or B-gap when needed.
weaknesses: Limited short-area athleticism to make adjustments. | Susceptible to slants and inside counters. | Struggles to stay low when making blocks in space. | Loses to opponent’s first hands. | Below-average lateral slide quickness to protect his edge. | Speed-to-power rushers back him into the pocket.

bio: A three-star recruit out of Logansport, Louisiana, Stephens signed with TCU. He played in eight games off the bench as a true freshman (2-58-29.0) and in 12 games in 2019 (11-157-14.3). He played in five contests in 2020 (1-5-5.0). Stephens then moved on to Louisiana, never starting there but getting more opportunities (13-167-12.8, four TDs in 14 games in 2021; 14-284-20.3, three TDs in 13 games in 2022). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Stephens, who played wide receiver in college, has the size and timed speed of a pass-catching tight end. His routes aren’t very refined but he’s loose-limbed and agile enough to make improvements in that area. Stephens flashes ball skills but the consistency of his hands is in question. Making a team early on could be tough, but he might find himself stashed on a practice squad if a team believes he has the toughness to improve as a blocker and play on special teams.
strengths: Outstanding size/length with solid explosiveness at pro day. | Athletic ability creates catch opportunities down the field. | Displays stack-and-track talent bringing in deep throws. | Keeps defender separated on fades with good hand positioning. | Above average high-point winner when needed.
weaknesses: Likely to require additional weight-room work to handle move to tight end. | Will need to prove himself as a blocker in the slot. | Posted more than 50 yards receiving in only one career game. | Needs to learn to disguise route intentions more effectively. | Had too many drops when the ball wasn’t perfectly placed.

overview: Lumpkin’s size and length will have some teams taking a close look to see if there is enough on tape to develop him as a heavy-handed Y tight end or even transition him inside to tackle. He is a decent blocker at the point of attack, with the traits and willingness to improve in that area. However, he’s unlikely to be much more than an occasional pass target sneaking out on play-action throws. His physical traits give him a chance to find a home on a practice squad while he continues to develop.
strengths: Rare combination of size and length at tight end. | Opens up his gait and picks up speed in space. | Uses frame to block out defenders on stop routes underneath. | Quality lateral movement for back-side cutoffs as zone blocker. | Flashed ability to kick out the edge or climb and seal linebackers. | Showed potential in pass protection.
weaknesses: Needs to add core strength and play with more grit. | Hand placement and bend at the point both need work. | Will lumber out of his stance and into the route at times. | Unlikely to beat NFL linebackers as a route-runner. | Not very physical after the catch.

bio: Gaines was a three-star recruit from Marquette University High School in the Milwaukee area. He redshirted in his first season with the Bruins, playing in one game in 2018. He earned an increased role at right guard in 2019, making one start in 12 games. Gaines started four of seven games played at the position in 2020 and started all 12 contests in 2021, showing versatility by lining up for the first two contests at center, one game at right tackle and nine others at right guard. He was an honorable mention All-Pac-12 Conference selection as a senior, starting all 13 games at right guard. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Move-blocking guard whose athleticism doesn’t guarantee consistent body control or balance in his play. Gaines is highly intelligent with a clear understanding of his duties on every snap. His hand placement can be a little sloppy, which diminishes his block sustain in the run game. While Gaines moves well as a run blocker, he struggles to stay under control and in front of opponents while mirroring. Gaines has the mental makeup coaches will like, but he needs to upgrade his protection technique and improve his core strength. He has backup guard/center potential.
strengths: Highly intelligent and assignment oriented. | Has started at center, guard and tackle. | Quick switch and capture of A-gap defender in run blitz. | Good radar and feel to find his targets on wide pulls. | Hits his landmarks with accuracy as zone blocker. | Actively searches for hand resets inside the rush rep.
weaknesses: Pass protection features subpar posture and balance. | Body control issues pop up too frequently on tape. | Leans into pass punch and opens himself for counters. | Slow to get feet sliding to protect his edges. | Hands lack focus and frequently slide off the opponent in run game.

bio: Ole Miss kept Mingo in-state as a four-star recruit from Brandon High School. He was a first-team all-state pick his senior year there and then stepped right into a starting job with Ole Miss, beginning all 12 games (12-172-14.3, one TD). His production increased as a sophomore (27-379-14.0, three TDs in 10 games, eight starts) and he played well in 2021 (22-346-15.7, three TDs in six starts) despite missing half the season with a broken left foot suffered in practice. Mingo started all 13 games in 2022, tying for the team lead with five receiving touchdowns (51-861-16.9). He set a school record with 247 receiving yards against Vanderbilt. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Big, strong slot receiver possessing the mental and physical toughness to outperform his speed limitations. The career production is nothing special, but it’s clear he’s put time and effort into his craft. He runs crisp, well-paced routes and ramps up his focus when it’s time to go get the football. A lack of separation burst and long speed could make for more contested catches, but he has the body type and willingness for that work. Mingo can get tough yards after the catch and is an above-average blocker. He has the skill level and demeanor to become a starting slot receiver for teams using 11 personnel (three WRs) as their base offense.
strengths: Imposing size with muscular build. | Easy to recognize he spends time on his craft. | Adequate footwork to slip press. | Finds his top speed quickly and continues to play at that speed. | Routes are run with attention to detail. | Works back aggressively to the throw. | Stellar ball tracking and catch focus downfield. | Makes use of his size and strength as run blocker.
weaknesses: Ordinary career production. | Lacks juice out of breaks to separate from tight man underneath. | Feet are efficient but lack suddenness. | Unable to find a second gear to run down deep balls. | Needs to get head around quicker on seam and over routes.

bio: Sutherland was a special teams stalwart for the Nittany Lions, joining quarterback Sean Clifford as the only four-time team captains in school history. He started once as a redshirt freshman (38 tackles, two for loss, one pass breakup), then played as a reserve and coverage units leader in 2019 (23 tackles in 13 games, two blocked punts versus Idaho) and 2020 (14 tackles, two for loss in nine games). The 2016 All-Washington D.C. Metro pick as a senior at Episcopal High School then started twice as a safety/linebacker in 2021 (24 tackles, two for loss, one interception) before moving to linebacker full-time in 2022 (38 tackles, 1.5 for loss in 13 games, eight starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Sutherland played a hybrid safety/linebacker spot for Penn State, with duties ranging from slot coverage to run fits. He posted impressive numbers at his pro day and has above-average special teams production during his career. While he was asked to handle a versatile role, the tape doesn’t show him shining in any one area. Sutherland will need to find a positional home -- possibly as a nickel/dime linebacker -- to complement his special teams potential at the next level.
strengths: Core special-teamer at Penn State. | Pro day testing numbers will garner attention from NFL teams. | Dives down into the fray with quick run-play diagnosis. | Deft upper-body turn helps him slip lead blockers. | Pursues running back with leverage to the sideline.
weaknesses: Hasn’t learned to play with his hands near the line of scrimmage. | Lacks size and strength for a full-time linebacker role. | Needs to play with greater fight-back when being blocked. | Closing speed in pursuit or as blitzer is just average. | Below-average feel for managing traffic in man coverage.

bio: Addison signed with Pittsburgh out of Tuscarora High School in Maryland and was an honorable mention All-ACC pick on offense in 2020, leading the Panthers in receiving (60-666-11.1, four TDs; 9-58-6.4 rushing; 2-39-19.5 kick returns; 2-15-7.5 punt returns). Addison became a star in 2021, winning the Biletnikoff Award as the nation's top receiver (joining former Pitt winners Antonio Bryant and Larry Fitzgerald) and garnering first-team Associated Press All-American and first-team All-ACC honors. He tied for the FBS lead with 17 receiving touchdowns, ranked sixth with 100 receptions and fourth with 1,593 receiving yards (15.9 per) in 14 games. Also, Addison was a third-team all-conference pick as an all-purpose player (7-56-8.0, one TD rushing; 12-185-15.4 punt returns). Transferring to USC for 2022 to play for head coach Lincoln Riley, Addison excelled. He was a first-team All-Pac-12 Conference selection as the Trojans' leading receiver (59-875-14.8, eight TDs; also 4-33-8.3 rushing, 4-19-4.8 punt returns in 11 starts) despite missing three games due to injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Inside/outside wideout with the speed and agility to work confidently on all three levels of the field, but lacking the size and catch strength generally associated with high-impact performers on the next level. Addison’s route running features acceleration, dynamic steering and sudden turns at a moment’s notice. While he can get to the spot effectively, he has trouble consistently winning battles when he has coverage company beside him. While Addison failed to make the same impact he did in 2021, his usage at Pitt might be a better indicator of the type of role and production he could be capable of on the next level.
strengths: Possesses athleticism and speed to work anywhere on the football field. | Early drive burst regardless of route depth. | Smart use of footwork defeats coverage leverage. | Accelerates through stems for separation to the post. | Good sink and foot agility getting in and out of breaks. | Ability to run complex routes with effectiveness. | Can be a slippery runner after the catch. | Punt return experience in all three seasons.
weaknesses: Only two touchdown catches over last seven games. | Route timing can be disrupted by handsy corners. | Limited catch radius for off-target throws. | Needs better timing in working back to throws. | Deep-ball tracking can be a little inconsistent. | Unable to create catch space downfield against size. | Average hand strength to finish through contact.

bio: The Fort Lauderdale native and top 100 overall recruit nationally committed to play for Urban Meyer at Ohio State but flipped to Alabama after Meyer left Columbus. Battle started four of 13 contests as a true freshman (30 tackles, two for loss, one interception) and was a leader for the secondary in the Tide's 2020 national championship season, starting 12 of 13 games and making 66 tackles (three for loss), one interception that was returned for a TD and four pass breakups. Battle garnered third-team Associated Press All-American and first-team All-SEC accolades in 2021, recording 84 tackles, tying for the team lead with three interceptions and tying for second in the FBS with two INTs returned for scores. He also added three pass breakups in 15 starts. In 2022, Battle was a third-team AP All-American and first-team all-conference pick after logging 71 tackles, one interception and two pass breakups in 13 games, all starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Battle offers the size, speed and pedigree to become a starter early in his NFL career. Film study shows a certain sageness to his game. He is usually where he needs to be on the field and helps his defense move on to the next play. He’s athletic enough for man coverage and is field-aware as a split safety. He’s not a thumper in run support and will miss tackles when he’s slow to find his positioning, but he typically finishes plays that are in front of him. Battle has the physical and mental makeup to upgrade a defense in need of steady safety play.
strengths: Versatility to cover the slot and support versus the run in the box. | Pursues ball-carriers with patience and adequate leverage. | Careful not to get trapped inside traffic near the line. | Steps downhill to tackle with toughness and technique. | Moves fluidly in coverage and transitions with good balance. | Instincts and processing to make plays. | Returned three of six career interceptions for touchdowns.
weaknesses: Run support consistency diminishes away from the line. | Average feel for reading runner’s open-field cuts. | Lacks high-end stopping punch against big backs. | Can be a little late breaking down to tackle in space. | Takes time to build up speed when ranging over the top. | Comes in a little too hot pursuing hitches to the flank.

bio: Howden was a football and track star as a senior at Desert Pines High School in California before heading to Minnesota. He started five of 13 appearances as a true freshman (45 tackles, one interception, three pass breakups). Howden started 12 times in 2019 (57 tackles, one interception, six pass breakups), all seven games in 2020 (37 tackles, one pass breakup) and 12 times in 2021 (43 tackles, 1.5 for loss, five pass breakups). He finished his career with an excellent fifth year, intercepting two passes and breaking up five others while making a career-high 58 tackles (3.5 for loss) in 13 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Howden is a football-savvy free safety with good instincts and play recognition but a lack of acceleration, which could create a plethora of problems for him on the pro level. He’s quick to diagnose the run, but will need to improve his tackle technique. A lack of recovery juice could get him mismatched on the pro game, but he sees route combinations well when allowed to play as a two-deep safety. Howden has played a lot of football and can help on special teams but needs to prove himself as a tester at the NFL Scouting Combine.
strengths: Team captain with 49 career starts. | Keys blocking scheme and immediately attacks run play. | Adequate patience when scraping with run play development. | Smooth hip flip to match route breaks with timing. | Intelligent and instinctive on the back end as deep safety. | Digests route combinations and flows with quarterback's eyes.
weaknesses: Backpedal is a little tight and upright. | Lacks length and speed to stay with vertical targets downfield. | Allows blocking receivers to get into his frame. | Has a tendency to overrun his pursuit leverage at times. | Feet show stall in lateral change of direction. | Unable to recover from a bad pursuit angle.

bio: Jones began his collegiate career at Nassau Community College in 2017 after matriculating there from Abraham Lincoln High School in Brooklyn, New York. He was a junior college All-American as a freshman and team captain his second year before transferring to Rhode Island. Jones played in four games off the bench in 2019 (one tackle) and started three games in the team's spring 2021 season (12 tackles, 1.5 for loss, four pass breakups). The Rams did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns. He had a breakout season in the fall of 2021, garnering second-team Associated Press All-American and second-team All-Colonial Athletic Association honors by ranking fourth in the FCS with six interceptions (also posting 36 tackles, team-high eight pass breakups in 11 starts). Jones was a first-team All-CAA pick last fall, recording 32 tackles and topping the squad with three interceptions and 12 pass breakups in 11 starts. He is Rhode Island's career leader with 33 passes defended. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Jones is a ball-hawking cornerback with the short-area quickness to be a factor in zone coverage. While he can press and play forms of man coverage, he’s much more effective in zone, where he allows his instincts to guide him. Jones’ ball skills come naturally and should follow him to the next level provided he can handle the step up in competition and finds a quality scheme fit.
strengths: Impressive ball skills and outstanding reaction quickness. | Posted eight interceptions and 20 pass breakups over the last two seasons. | Reads quarterback with accuracy from zone. | Fluid hips with sudden burst to close on the throw. | Plays passing lanes and is surehanded on 50/50 battles. | Maintains contain positioning as run defender.
weaknesses: Loses early ground when flipping to chase the vertical route. | Needs to keep feet under him when driving downhill. | Inconsistent ball recognition from trail position. | Needs to get off perimeter blocks more quickly in run support.

bio: The South Carolina Offensive Lineman of the Year at Dorman High School as a senior redshirted in his first year at Clemson, playing in three games as a reserve for the national champions. McFadden played in 14 games as a reserve and on special teams in 2019. McFadden played well enough in 12 starts at right tackle in 2020 to earn honorable mention All-ACC notice from league coaches. He was a second-team all-conference selection for his play in 13 starts at left tackle in 2021 before winning the Jacobs Blocking Trophy as the league's top blocker in 14 starts on the blindside in 2022. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Three-year starter and team captain with experience at both tackle spots. McFadden lacks the height/length to stay at tackle in the NFL, but he has the broad frame and run-blocking acumen to fit as a guard. He’s firm and accurate into blocks using good footwork to drive and turn opponents. He lacks ideal mass and will get dumped by twitchy run defenders at times. His protection experience at tackle is a big plus in his favor, but he still needs to fire his hands with better efficiency and from a tighter track. McFadden is a reliable prospect lacking desired measurables but has the chance to become a good backup with eventual starter potential.
strengths: Broad through upper and lower body with good lean mass. | Balanced and firm into initial contact as run blocker. | Drive blocks with ability to exploit defender’s weight shifts. | Typically keeps defender centered in his power zone. | Climbs to second level with control. | Pass protection experience at tackle is a big plus. | Flashes early hands to draw out rusher’s hands and counter them. | Adequate hand resets to come under and inside opponent’s hands.
weaknesses: Swings hands wide with too many pass punches. | Needs to play under his pads in pass pro and as run blocker. | Deadens slide feet at the top of the rush. | Pad level rises when working laterally in run game. | Punched and discarded quickly by Florida State’s Jared Verse. | Has trouble latching into opponent’s pads with his hands.

bio: Mims made a grand entrance to the Bulldogs in 2017, leading the team with 627 rushing yards (151 carries, 4.2 per; also 14-143-10.2 receiving) and scoring six times in 14 games (three starts) just one year after rushing for 2,388 yards as the South Bay/Peninsula Offensive Player of the Year at Menlo-Atherton High School. He played in 12 games, starting five, as a sophomore (113-436-3.9, six TDs rushing; 21-286-13.6, two TDs receiving) but missed the final two games that year and the entire 2019 campaign with an ankle injury. Mims returned as a reserve in 2020 (28-145-5.2, one TD rushing; 10-92-9.2 receiving in six games, one start) and then returned to his normal workload in 2021 (127-710-5.6, team-high six TDs rushing; 25-324-13.0, four TDs receiving; 13-285-21.9 kick returns). He made the most of his final season at Fresno with a first-team All-Mountain West Conference campaign, leading the team with 1,372 rushing yards and 18 scores (261 carries, 5.3 per) and contributing as a receiver (21-126-6.0, one TD) in 14 starts. He was the Jimmy Kimmel LA Bowl Offensive MVP (18-209-11.6, two TDs rushing; 2-27-13.5 receiving) in the win over Washington State. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Mims runs with solid vision and good toughness to find yardage that is on the field for him. He can make a defender miss in space, but he doesn’t possess the sudden acceleration to blaze through the line of scrimmage or stack multiple cuts and keep runs going without tacklers finding him. He has some talent as an interior runner but needs to pick up the pace and become a little more decisive early on. He has some pass protection ability but might not catch the ball well enough for third-down consideration, which could hurt his chances of making a team.
strengths: Chiseled frame with proportional, athletic build. | Has not fumbled an offensive touch since the 2017 season, per PFF. | Processes fairly quickly and adjusts accordingly. | Navigates interior terrain with smooth change of direction. | Runs with good bend and forward lean to fall forward. | Makes effort to drive through initial contact as ball-carrier.
weaknesses: Below-average acceleration getting up to the second level. | Tendency to dance early in the run could be an issue in NFL. | Unable to find getaway gear after making lateral cuts. | Doesn’t have desired speed for outside runs. | Catching the ball does not come naturally.

bio: Perryman grew up in California, starring at running back and free safety at Hanford High School. He signed with Cal-Davis in 2017, redshirting that fall. He started one game in 2018 (20 tackles, two interceptions, three pass breakups in 13 appearances) and 11 contests in 2019 (41 tackles, one interception, two pass breakups). The school did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID concerns. Perryman garnered first-team All-Big Sky Conference honors in the spring (16 tackles, two pass breakups) and fall of 2021, when he led the Aggies with 12 pass breakups (63 tackles, 2.5 for loss, one interception in 12 starts). He transferred to Washington for 2022, starting 10 games (37 tackles, one pass breakup) and missed three with a leg injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Perryman looked overwhelmed in coverage after making the jump in competition to the Pac-12 last season. He has an NFL frame, but he lacks the fluidity and overall coverage instincts needed to stay connected to pro route runners. His physicality could create an opportunity for a safety transition, but he might not be able to make it as an NFL cornerback.
strengths: Possesses NFL size and length on the perimeter. | Shows ability to plant and drive on throws underneath from side shuffle. | Physical striker when attacking pass-catchers. | Sees what he hits in run support with aggressive leg attacks. | Experienced as a successful gunner at Cal-Davis.
weaknesses: Had almost no on-ball production in 10 starts for Washington last season. | Gets turned by press release. | Backpedal is too upright and bumpy. | Below average route anticipation and transitions. | Loses track of receivers during secondary effort. | Dropped a plethora of would-be interceptions during his career.

bio: Rhodes signed with South Carolina out of Creekside High School in Georgia, playing in four games as a reserve after a redshirt year. He started 10 of 12 appearances at left guard for the Gamecocks in 2019. He initially chose to opt out of the 2020 season due to COVID-19 concerns, but eventually returned to the team, playing in four games off the bench. He transferred to Ole Miss for 2021, starting once at left guard among 13 games played, and changed addresses again for 2022. He started 11 games for Arkansas State last fall, receiving honorable mention All-Sun Belt Conference honors for his efforts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Rhodes has five-star physical traits. He flashes power at the point of attack, but he lacks the functional athleticism to play laterally or in space and will struggle to mirror NFL competition.
strengths: Girthy, broad frame with extremely long arms. | Knocks the nose tackle off-balance on down blocks. | Good power for work on double teams. | Finishes run blocks. | Gets long arms out and engages quickly in protection.
weaknesses: Heavy, lumbering feet getting out of his stance. | Lacks functionality once he’s asked to expand the work area. | Edge-to-edge rushers will beat him moving across his face. | Hip tightness prevents desired recoveries in pass pro.

bio: Riley starred at Riverside High School in North Carolina and then moved to Chapel Hill to play for UNC. He played in five games as a true freshman (six tackles). He did not play in 2018. Riley played at Garden City Community College in 2019 and then was signed by Nebraska, where he played as a reserve in six games in 2020 (one tackle) and 10 games the next fall (seven tackles, one for loss). The move to Oregon for his final college season paid off, as he started all 13 contests and posted a career-high 21 tackles (1.5 for loss). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Riley is a rotational nose tackle with a proportional frame carrying good thickness. He’s capable of battling against double teams and absorbing contact, but he needs to improve his technique and work on taking control of the action. He’s primarily a block-eater and is unlikely to make many plays, but his size will be appealing.
strengths: Tall, wide and proportional frame. | Possesses mass and length as a two-gapper. | Shows potential to muddy the waters as a run defender. | Adequate knockback pop into first contact.
weaknesses: Took just 534 snaps in the FBS, per PFF. | Will need to improve technique to handle NFL blockers. | Posted very little production during his career in the FBS.

bio: Ramirez signed with Arizona out of Auburndale High School, where he was an All-Florida pick as a senior. He redshirted the 2017 season before racking up eight sacks in 12 games for Riverside City College the following fall. Joining EMU for 2019, he played in four games as a reserve (no statistics). Ramirez garnered third-team All-MAC honors the next two seasons, starting all six games in the shortened 2020 campaign (27 tackles, 2.5 for loss with two sacks) and leading the Eagles with 12 tackles for loss with 6.5 sacks (among 63 total tackles) and three forced fumbles in 13 games with eight starts in 2021. He took advantage of the extra year of eligibility awarded all players due to the pandemic, winning 2022 MAC Defensive Player of the Year and third-team Associated Press All-American honors by ranking second in the FBS with 12 sacks and tying for fourth with 19.5 tackles for loss while also posting 66 total tackles, breaking up two passes and forcing two fumbles in 13 games (11 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ramirez’s below-average run defense could make it difficult for him to see the field early in his career, but he blends a hot motor and natural rush talent that could entice teams willing to continue his development in both phases. He’s agile with the ability to gather and chase with quickness once he finds an advantage inside the pocket. He can add strength and technique to improve his block take-on, but he'll also need to show more grit. Ramirez has the potential to be drafted later on Day 3; natural pass rushers always have a shot to grow and become productive pros.
strengths: Recorded 31.5 tackles for loss and 18.5 sacks in the last two seasons. | Punches through tight end to separate at the point. | Plays with unyielding pursuit of the football. | Times up snap and charges upfield to rush. | Effective stab-and-swipe rush move to win the edge. | Able to gather his feet and flatten to the quarterback. | Conscientious working to pocket depth and dropping back under.
weaknesses: Gets outside shoulder covered and loses his contain. | Unable to anchor and prevent being widened out by tackles. | Below-average aggression attacking blockers with force. | Inconsistent to unglue from latched blocks. | Long-arm bully move runs out of steam against size. | Needs to activate hands more quickly to elude punch.

bio: Ngata (pronounced enn-GOT-uh) was a five-star recruit who helped Folsom High School win a state title his senior year. He caught 17 passes for 240 yards and three scores in 15 games as a true freshman. However, an abdominal injury suffered in the 2020 opener limited him to three starts in seven contests (7-83-11.9). Ngata played in nine games with eight starts (23-438-19.0, one TD) in 2021, missing four games due to a foot injury. He started all 14 games in 2022, catching 41 passes for 526 yards (12.8 per) and two scores. His brother, Ariel, played linebacker at Washington and then transferred to Sacramento State. Another brother, Daniyel, was a four-star running back recruit who signed with Arizona State and then transferred to Washington. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Former five-star prospect with quality size, speed and length but an inability to separate from press-man coverage. Ngata is a smooth pass-catcher and has decent ball skills, but it takes him too long to elude press. When he gets into the route, it will be tough for him to uncover against NFL quickness and coverage talent.
strengths: Former five-star signee with pro size and length. | Solid performances in ACC title game and Orange Bowl. | Uses his frame to hold off clingy cornerbacks. | Plucks throws with good hand extension. | Above-average hand-eye coordination working into the middle. | Returned kicks as a freshman.
weaknesses: Battled injuries in 2020 and 2021. | Slow to find his release against press. | Lacks the early acceleration to run past his man. | Below-average quickness getting into his breaks. | One-speed route runner unable to outmaneuver tight man coverage.

bio: Downs was rated as one of the top 100 recruits in the 2020 class nationally after a stellar career in football (first-team all-state) and track (top five in the triple and long jumps at the state meet his sophomore year) at North Gwinnett High School in Georgia. He signed with North Carolina in part to play for his uncle and former UNC and NFL star corner, Dre Bly, who was the defensive backs coach at the time. Downs played in 10 games off the bench as a true freshman (7-119-17.0, three TDs) and then came into his own the 2021, garnering first-team All-ACC honors by ranking fifth in the FBS with 101 receptions and 10th with 1,335 receiving yards. He also led Carolina with eight receiving touchdowns in 13 games (12 starts) and returned punts (16-156-9.8). Downs earned second-team Associated Press All-American and first-team all-conference honors as a receiver in 2022, topping the squad with 94 receptions for 1,029 yards (11.0 per) and tying for seventh nationally with 11 touchdowns in 11 starts. He was also a second-team All-ACC pick as an all-purpose player (10-133-13.3 punt returns). He missed two games due to injury and opted out of the team's bowl game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Free-flowing athlete with dynamic footwork and an instinctive feel for how to elude opponents. Downs posted off-the-charts production over the last two seasons as an undersized slot with an oversized will. His confidence jumps off the tape and he has proven himself to be better at catching through contact than you might expect. While his route running is effective and fun to watch, coaches will need him to become more disciplined and efficient in order to maintain the timing of play designs. Downs might not have prototypical size, but he’s well-positioned to keep stacking catches and making plays as a starting NFL slot receiver.
strengths: Supremely confident with outstanding production over last two seasons. | Appears to have both quickness and long speed. | Tempo changes create unease for man coverage. | Separation burst gains space through turns/cuts. | Footwork and change of direction are sudden and sharp. | Uses athleticism to elude defenders. | Leaps and adjusts to pick throws off defender’s head. | Surprising catch toughness for his size. | Slippery when asked to return punts.
weaknesses: Below average build working into the middle. | Can be slowed by a physical press corner. | Needs to be more disciplined in route running. | Will leave routes unfinished at times. | Struggled with focus drops at times during career. | Unable to make a difference as a run blocker.

bio: Hayes signed with FCS powerhouse North Dakota State after starring at Florida's Lake Gibson High School. He played in all 15 games as a true freshman (15 tackles, three pass breakups), starting the national title victory over James Madison. Hayes started twice in 15 appearances in 2018 (28 tackles, nine on special teams), recording a tackle for loss and one of his three pass breakups for the year in the win over Eastern Washington in the 2018 FCS Championship Game. He helped the team win a third straight title in 2019, garnering second-team All-Missouri Valley Football Conference honors (59 tackles, two for loss, two interceptions, 10 pass breakups in 16 starts). Hayes started six games in the Bison's six-game 2020-21 season (30 tackles, three pass breakups) before heading to the transfer portal. He landed at Virginia for 2021 (one tackle in three games) before moving on to play for former NDSU head coach Chris Klieman at Kansas State for his final campaign. He moved from corner to safety for the Wildcats, starting 13 games (71 tackles, 5.5 for loss, seven pass breakups). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Hayes has adequate physical and athletic measurables to play slot cornerback, but he might need to bulk up to play safety. He is active against the run and the pass, but his inconsistency as a tackler could make it challenging for him to stick on a roster.
strengths: Active and athletic. | Ability to play in the slot or at safety. | Good speed for man-coverage duties. | Possesses traits to play on special teams.
weaknesses: Lacks ideal frame as an NFL safety candidate. | Missed too many tackles in 2022. | Needs to play with better discipline and technique as tackler.

bio: Vann arrived at South Carolina as a top 150 national recruit from Tucker, Georgia. He started one game as a true freshman (18-118-6.6, one TD in 13 games), three times as a sophomore (19-171-9.0 receiving; 2-24 punt returns in nine contests) and four times in 2020 (10-88-8.8, one TD in 10 appearances). Vann was the Gamecocks' top receiver in 2022 (43-679-15.8, five TDs receiving; 5-63-12.6 rushing; 7-64-9.1 punt returns), starting 12 of 13 games played. He played in 12 games as a reserve in 2022 (18-296-16.4, three TDs receiving; 10-151-15.1 punt returns). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Vann has played inside and outside; he could end up doing the same as a pro. He ran well at his pro day, but his play speed can be inconsistent on tape. He has average size and strength. Also, he relies on athletic ability over positioning savvy to battle for contested catches. The production was fairly average at South Carolina, but his testing and 2021 tape could play to his favor.
strengths: Ran well and showed off explosiveness in pro day testing. | Switches up route tempos to keep defensive backs guessing. | Able to plant and accelerate quickly when beating press. | Showed off second gear against Georgia in 2021. | Averaged 15.1 yards per punt return in 2022.
weaknesses: Pops upright getting into his breaks underneath. | Needs to break off out routes at tighter angles. | Average burst to separate at the break points. | Inconsistent adjusting positioning and speed against ball challenges. | Average talent after the catch.

bio: Whyle (pronounced why-lee) was offered by Big Ten, SEC and ACC schools as a top-10 tight end prospect out of La Salle High School but decided to stay home in Cincinnati to play for coach Luke Fickell. He redshirted in 2018, playing in four late-season games without catching a pass. He caught two passes for 51 yards (25.5 per) in 2019, then broke out in 2020, receiving second-team All-American Athletic Conference honors by catching a team-high six touchdowns (28-353-12.6). Whyle received honorable mention all-league notice in 2021, starting eight of 14 games played (26-332-12.8, six TDs). He was a first-team All-AAC selection in his final campaign (32-326-10.2, three TDs in 12 games, 10 starts), opting out of the Fenway Bowl to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Smooth, athletic pass-catcher with the competitiveness to battle for playing time in the league. Whyle is an average route runner who is forced to tap the brakes when facing physical coverage, but he has the tools to uncover as a pro. He possesses the jump-ball prowess to mismatch defensive backs near the goal line and can be a nice safety blanket on pitch-and-catch throws underneath. He needs to keep adding play strength to match the rigors of the position and is better suited as a move blocker than tenacious in-line blocker near the line of scrimmage. Whyle appears to be a middle-round prospect for teams seeking an F tight end or H-back with starting upside.
strengths: Changes gears to separate on route turns. | Steps on top of safety before breaking off post routes. | Loose upper and lower body allows for easy ball adjustments. | Recognizes lurking zone defenders and sinks into safe spaces for QB. | Excellent timing as high-point pass-catcher. | Unafraid to charge in and stick his nose into blocks. | Fits into lead blocks with proper angles to open a crease. | Good use of length and athleticism as blocker on the move.
weaknesses: Long but somewhat spindly in his lower half. | Acceleration into his route is non-threatening to defenders. | Slowed by redirection and press. | Routes can become loose and unfocused at times. | Below average success rate hauling in contested catches. | Will struggle to find proper leverage as run blocker. | Power ends can have success knocking him off his base.

bio: Rated as one of the top 20 guard prospects nationally, Gwyn signed with South Carolina for the 2018 season. The first-team All-North Carolina pick from Harding University High School redshirted that season due to a foot injury that required surgery, playing in one game off the bench. He stepped in to start 11 of 12 games played in 2019, all 10 contests of the 2020 campaign and all 13 of the 2021 season at right guard. SEC coaches voted him second-team all-conference for his play as a senior in 13 starts at that right guard spot. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Gwyn is a solid football player, but his lack of size and length is a major hindrance relative to staying at guard. He’ll likely need to prove he can snap and play center, where he will still be considered undersized. He’s a tenacious run blocker who can operate in multiple schemes but might not be able to shine in any of them. Gwyn plays with a firm base and good body control in protection but lacks the length and range to consistently protect gaps. Gwyn will be a one-position player, but he has enough talent and technique to compete for a roster spot at center.
strengths: Four-year starter and well-respected teammate. | Adequate first-step quickness as zone- and pull-blocker. | Plays under his pads and with body control. | Hand strength and foot movement to stay connected to blocks. | Very firm when standing up to power rushers. | Able to open his hips and slide to recovery in pass sets.
weaknesses: Undersized with short arms. | Unable to move bodies around as a drive blocker. | Will struggle to keep big guys from crossing his face. | Not enough range to protect widening rush gaps. | Short arms allow rushers to work around his pass mirror.

bio: Scruggs helped Cathedral Prep High School win back-to-back state titles. He received first-team all-state and Lineman of the Year accolades before heading to Happy Valley. He redshirted in 2018, playing in one game off the bench. Scruggs suffered a broken back in a car accident prior to 2019 spring practices. He spent months in a back brace and acted as a de facto coach for the line during his recovery. He played in seven games as a reserve in 2020, earning a team award for inspiring his teammates. Finally able to start in 2021, Scruggs was named honorable mention All-Big Ten Conference for his play in 13 contests. He was a third-team selection as a senior, starting all 13 games at center. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A two-year starter with center/guard versatility, Scruggs is dependable and consistent in carrying out his assignment to the best of his ability. He plays like a block of granite that is difficult to push back or knock off-balance, but he’s more of a neutralizer than road grader. He plays with solid technique and possesses the play strength to hold his own in the middle. The lack of foot quickness shows up with athletic defenders leaking around his edges and that issue could be exacerbated if teams play him at guard. Scruggs has the potential to go from backup to eventual starter if the situation is right.
strengths: Team captain. | Proportionally dense through his limbs. | Latches in with strong hands and a wide base. | Can hold strong in one-on-one power swaps. | Inside hands to promote a strong core. | Hands are patient in pass sets. | Centers pass rusher with square punch. | Keeps head on a swivel looking for danger.
weaknesses: Below average snap-to-step quickness. | Very average lateral quickness to seal the nose tackle. | More wall-off than drive blocker. | Foot slide to secure blocks is lacking. | Unable to flip hips for recovery blocks. | Could struggle to redirect and pick up twisters. | Needs to find quicker hand resets in pass protection.

bio: Hill was an all-conference quarterback at Pine Forest High School in North Carolina. He was a reserve pass-catcher his first two years at Campbell (1-5-5.0 in 11 games in 2018; 6-85-14.2 in 11 games in 2019). He started all four games that Campbell played in 2020 (6-102-17.0). He did the same for all 11 games in 2021 (34-367-10.8, two TDs) and 2022 (38-659-17.3, five TDs), topping the Camels in receiving as a senior and garnering first-team All-Big South Conference honors both seasons. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Tight end prospect who plays his position with the physicality teams will be looking for. Hill has average hands and short-area quickness. He can catch through contact, but he will drop some very catchable ones. He can play in the slot or attached as a wing. He comes off the ball ready to hit and drive until the whistle sounds. Hill’s athletic testing and willingness as a blocker help his chances of making a team.
strengths: Excellent feel for attacking zone coverage. | Avoids route traffic to maintain timing of the pattern. | Makes improvisational route extensions when needed. | Above-average toughness as a point-of-attack blocker. | Dips and explodes hips into contact. | Gives good effort to sustain block with grit and hand strength.
weaknesses: Smaller than desired as an in-line blocker. | Needs to maintain patience and control when blocking. | Will be average in challenging man coverage down the seam. | Average success rate as a hands-catcher. | Needs to give greater effort working back to the throw.

bio: Brents signed with Iowa as a top 30 cornerback nationally and completed his career at Warner Central High School in Indianapolis as a three-time first-team all-conference pick. He started five of 11 appearances as a true freshman (13 tackles, one interception, three pass breakups) but had to redshirt the 2019 season after suffering a knee injury in fall camp (playing in one game, no statistics). Brents came off the bench for seven contests in 2020 (four tackles, one pass breakup) before transferring to Kansas State for the 2021 season. He was an honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference selection in his first year with the Wildcats, recording 49 tackles, three for loss, one interception and two pass breakups while starting all 13 games. Brents ascended to first-team all-Big 12 in 2022, leading K-State with four interceptions and recording 45 tackles (3.5 for loss) and four pass breakups in 14 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Brents is a classic zone cover corner with an outstanding blend of size, length and leaping ability. He has the disruptive traits to reroute the release and the dog in him to handle his business in run support. He can play some press-man on a vertical plane but lacks the top-end speed and pattern matching to play in that scheme full-time. Brents needs to maintain eye discipline from zone but has the ball skills to win a battle for the pass when he’s in position. While he’s likely to be targeted in the draft as a zone-based corner, he has the instincts and demeanor to make a move to safety if needed.
strengths: Rare blend of size and length at cornerback. | Can jab and maintain contact through press release. | Spies quarterback from side-shuffle and overlaps his coverage. | Digests route combination cleanly from zone. | Able to partition off catch space on deep sideline throw. | Explosive leaps to win the high-point battle. | Aggressive attacker as a run supporter. | Springs from his hips to wrap up ball-carrier.
weaknesses: Can be juked out of position matching press release. | Struggles to stay in phase through pattern breaks. | Will lose ground once the route becomes a foot race. | Loses track of wideout when zone focus lingers on quarterback. | False steps when planting to drive from top of the drop. | Playmaking mindset can be exploited by misdirection. | Feet stall instead of running through the tackle.

bio: Ford moved across the country, matriculating from Cox Hill High School in North Carolina to Golden West Community College in California. He played for two seasons there, then signed with Louisville for the 2019 season. Ford redshirted that fall due to injury and then decided to move on to Montana. The Grizzlies did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns, but Ford played in both of the team's games in the spring of 2021 (nine tackles, 2.5 for loss). The following fall, he burst onto NFL scouts' radars by leading all NCAA divisions with nine interceptions, returning two for touchdowns. He garnered first-team Associated Press FCS All-American, first-team All-Big Sky Conference and Big Sky Newcomer of the Year accolades. He posted an interception in eight straight games and tied for the Montana lead with 11 pass breakups to go along with 41 tackles, two for loss with one sack in 13 starts. Ford was a second-team AP FCS All-American and first-team all-conference selection in 2022, recording 34 tackles, intercepting a team-high two passes and breaking up five others. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Ford has the instincts and ball skills to find opportunities to make plays on the football. He’s a little erratic from press and might not have the speed to recover from trail positioning, but he does a nice job of attacking throws with his eyes forward. He has a chance to compete for a back-end roster spot on a team with a zone-heavy defense.
strengths: Recorded 11 interceptions in his final two seasons, including nine in 2021.* Eyes the quarterback and makes instant reads on the release.* Makes plays on the ball by overlapping zone coverages.* Springy drive steps close out distance to the throw.* Above-average ball skills when challenging the 50/50 ball.
weaknesses: Segmented backpedal from press.* Below-average foot agility matching press release.* Closing burst from off-man is below average.* Will stay behind once he falls behind to speedsters.* Drag-down tackler who needs to wrap up more often.

bio: Marshall signed with Louisville out of the Georgia Prep Sports Academy. He redshirted in 2017, then played as a reserve the next two seasons (no statistics in nine games in 2018; 6-135-22.5 in 10 games in 2019). Marshall got three starts in 2020 (7-87-12.4 in 10 appearances) and then started 12 games in 2021 (23-322-14.0, one TD) before entering the transfer portal. He joined Buffalo for 2022, leading the Bulls with 64 receptions for 837 yards (13.1 per) and nine scores in 13 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: On paper, Marshall has size, speed and an explosive vertical leap. When the tape is turned on, it is easy to see the size and leaping talent, but the play speed can be harder to find in the context of the offense. The build-up speed is fine for vertical routes, but Marshall is sluggish getting off press and lacks the fluidity/quickness to run routes that will create throwing windows for quarterbacks. His high contested-targets total figures to follow him to the next level, which will make it hard for him to stick on a roster.
strengths: Possesses a nice blend of size, speed and explosiveness. | Natural ball-tracking instincts down the field. | Varies speed as he tracks the ball to capture winning body positioning. | Catches with good focus and timing on jump balls. | Above-average feel for using frame to wall-off defenders.
weaknesses: Initial take-off into the route can be plodding and gradual. | Gives press cornerbacks an accessible target. | Struggled winning contested-catch battles against Maryland corners in 2022. | Tight-hipped and bumpy getting through route transitions.

bio: Shorter earned second-team USA Today All-USA honors and New Jersey's Offensive Player of the Year his senior season at South Brunswick High School. He was rated the top receiver prospect in the country before signing with Penn State for 2018 but redshirted that fall (3-20-6.7 in four games) because he missed midseason contests due to injury. He played in 10 games with five starts for the Nittany Lions in 2019 (12-137-11.4) but fought through injuries and was benched after dropping passes during the season.
