He possesses premium running talent for zone-read and quarterback draws, and he can turn a lack of contain into a huge play with his legs. Teams will need to decide how Cunningham would fit into an offense, but his ability to make explosive plays with his legs should not be discounted.
strengths: Dynamic athlete with intriguing dual-threat capabilities. | Stresses defenses from RPO and zone-read looks. | Decent passing accuracy when in rhythm. | Instant burst to outrace pursuit to the corner. | Vision like a running back in the open field. | Consistently eludes tacklers in all areas of the field.
weaknesses: Angular build with narrow hips and slender frame. | Completed just 31 percent of his deep throws in 2022, per PFF. | Stares coverage into his intermediate targets. | Failed to build on a solid first season in 2019.

bio: Heath was rated one of the top 175 prospects in the country for his efforts at Callaway High School in Mississippi. He stayed in the Magnolia State to play at Copiah-Lincoln Community College for two years, eventually becoming a top 10 overall junior college recruit in the 2019 class. Mississippi State signed Heath, and he started six times for the Bulldogs in 2020 (37-307-8.3, three TDs in 10 games) and three times in 2021 (34-442-13.0, five TDs in 11 contests) before moving on to his third college in the state, Ole Miss. He led the team with 60 receptions for 971 yards (16.2 per) and tied for the team lead with five touchdown catches in 13 games with 12 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: The size and length are appealing, as is the potential to improve his contested-catch success rate, but Heath lacks the burst to back coverages off or separate consistently against press-man. The ball skills show up on tape, but he must become a consistent ball-winner and play to his size. Heath has Day 3 draft potential.
strengths: Saw a steep jump in reception production in 2022. | Nice stair-step technique to back coverage off. | Locates deep throws and alters speed and positioning to grab the ball. | Possesses the size and length to rise above cornerbacks on jump balls. | Does well focusing on dropping his feet near the sideline on catches. | Has a chance to become a reliable winner on back-shoulder throws.
weaknesses: Lacks take-off burst and has predictable outside release. | Needs to make route breaks and turns with better knee bend. | Dropped too many contested catches that hit him in the hands. | Below-average run-after-catch ability.

bio: Knowles redshirted the 2018 season at Kansas State, though he started one of four games played that fall (10-100-10.0, two TDs). The former all-district player from Lake Ridge High School in Texas started eight of 11 games played in 2019 (27-397-14.7, three TDs receiving; 7-70-10.0 rushing; 6-222-37.0, TD kick returns) and started nine contests in 2020 (13-204-15.7, three TDs receiving; 6-100-16.7, one TD rushing; 11-203-18.5 kick returns). Knowles had his best year as a junior in 2021, earning honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference notice as a receiver (29-441-15.2, four TDs in 13 games, 11 starts) and first-team all-conference accolades as a return specialist after tying for second in the FBS with two kickoff returns for touchdowns (20-662-33.1). He was a second-team pick at receiver in 2022, topping the Wildcats with 48 receptions for 725 yards (15.1) while scoring twice in 14 games with 11 starts. Knowles returned kicks in his final college season (23-592-25.7), as well. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Perimeter receiver with adequate measurables and above-average value as a kick returner. Knowles is an angular route runner who is much more effective on longer-developing routes that allow him to win with tempo through turns. Lacking suddenness, he will struggle beating press and uncovering underneath. He requires a runway to find his speed on run-after-catch throws. Knowles is athletic and smooth as a pass-catcher but might be limited to a role as a potential WR5/6 with kick return value.
strengths: Talented kick returner with three career touchdowns. | Angular movements are rhythmic and connected. | Able to get through route turns with even tempo. | Catches with soft hands and good extension to the throw. | Athletic and smooth catching in space. | Makes well-timed leaps to find the high point.
weaknesses: Detoured and rerouted by press. | Not equipped to beat tight man with early burst. | Slow to gather feet and break from drive phase. | Allows coverage to crowd him at the top of the route. | Needs to consistently finish his routes. | Takes time to find acceleration after the catch.

collegeNames: University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff
bio: Evans played at C.E. King High School in Houston before enrolling at Arkansas-Pine Bluff for the 2018 season. He started the final two contests of his true freshman season, playing in nine games overall. Evans earned first-team All-Southwestern Athletic Conference honors in 2019, starting all 11 games at left tackle. The school did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns. Evans started all five games in the team's spring season, garnering first-team HBCU All-American accolades. He started all 11 games on the blind side again in 2021, earning first-team all-conference honors. After starting nine games at left tackle as a senior in 2022, Evans received second-team Associated Press FCS All-American and first-team All-SWAC notice. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Feisty tackle-to-guard prospect who plays with the desired mindset and tenacity that evaluators will love. Evans is a hardworking run blocker with strong hands and ample leg drive but fails to create consistent leverage at the point of attack. He’s a willing combatant in both the run and pass game but lacks consistent body control and hand usage. He has the potential to be a make-it player, but the pass protection must significantly improve.
strengths: Consistently takes the fight to defender through the whistle. | Fits into blocks with a forceful thud. | Strong desire to move defenders with effort and leg drive. | Big hands lock into opponent’s pads. | Keeps feet sliding with rusher around the arc. | Able to get into space and help in the screen game.
weaknesses: Below average NFL size and mass. | Must learn to play lower and with better leverage. | Hand usage and placement are sloppy in the run game. | Lacking desired body control and reactive agility. | Gets knocked back and out of position against power rushers. | Will need to play with more consistent inside hands.

bio: Ford caught nine touchdowns as a senior at Ballard High School before walking on at his hometown school. He played in four games as a redshirt freshman in 2018 (no statistics) before earning a scholarship and a full-time starting role for 2019 (20-292-14.6, seven TDs in 13 games). Ford started nine of 10 games played in 2020 (25-309-12.4, six TDs) and then garnered third-team All-ACC honors after leading the Cardinals with 49 receptions and 550 receiving yards, scoring twice in 13 starts. He was an honorable mention all-league selection in his sixth season with Louisville, leading the squad with three receiving touchdowns (33-434-13.2) in 13 games with 11 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Productive tight end who has posted solid numbers for four consecutive years. Ford is lacking functional size and strength for the position, so he might need a highly specific role that allows him to primarily act as a pass-catcher. He’s a willing run blocker with decent technique and might have the ability to expand his role as a move blocker in space. Ford has good speed to separate on intermediate routes. He displays good toughness and focus on contested catches. He has Day 3 potential on tape, but size concerns could force him to earn his way as an undrafted free agent.
strengths: Play speed to accelerate past linebackers and uncover. | Good tempo with smooth footwork through route turns. | Makes easy adjustments to throws outside his frame. | Finishes catches through solid contact. | Looks like a big wideout when the ball is in his hands.
weaknesses: Lacks NFL-caliber size; lean body type will require additional mass and muscle. | Missing pure power to beat NFL edge defenders as base blocker. | Fairly limited route-tree experience. | Could have issues getting off the line if redirected.

bio: Mapu starred at Hawthorne High School in California before heading to Sacramento State in 2017, redshirting his first year with the program. He played in five games in 2018 (six tackles) and 11 games in 2019 (18 tackles, one interception, two starts). The team did not play in 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns. Mapu earned second-team All-Big Sky Conference accolades the next fall after leading the Hornets with four interceptions and 10 pass breakups (also posting 65 tackles, 5.5 for loss in 12 starts). He was a first-team Associated Press FCS All-American and the Big Sky Conference Defensive Player of the Year in 2022, filling the stat sheet in 13 starts (76 tackles, 6.5 for loss, two interceptions, four pass breakups, one blocked kick). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Mapu has been praised for his versatility, but he might need to prove he can excel in at least one department -- whether in run support or in coverage -- at the next level. He lacks short-area athleticism and long speed, so his man coverage might be limited to tight ends. He is highly instinctive from short zone and is a very willing hitter when playing near the box. It won’t be a surprise if Mapu adds weight and locks in as a backup weakside linebacker in a 4-3 defense as a pro.
strengths: Big safety with the ability to help support the run. | Plays with desired run-and-hit mentality. | Run-through tackler. | Picked off six passes over the last two seasons. | Outstanding reading quarterback from short zone. | Size and strength to cover Y tight ends in space.
weaknesses: Allows blockers to get into his frame in the box. | Feet are heavy in his short-area movements. | Questionable pursuit speed when the play flows wide. | Needs to prove he has a clean position fit.

bio: Mims originally committed to Stanford as a four-star recruit from Lone Star High School, where he set a national record with 2,629 receiving yards (117 catches, 32 TDs) as a senior as well as the Texas state record with 5,485 career receiving yards. He did not disappoint as a true freshman in 2020, leading the Sooners with 610 yards (16.5 per) and nine touchdowns receiving and tying for the team lead with 37 receptions in 11 games (one start). Mims was an honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference selection in 2021, ranking fourth in the FBS with 22.0 yards per catch and topping his squad with 32 receptions for 705 yards (scoring five times). He garnered first-team all-league notice as a junior, topping his squad with 54 receptions for 1,083 yards (ranking sixth in the country with 20.1 per) and six scores in 13 games with 12 starts. Mims also returned kicks (3-70-23.3) and punts (33-391-11.8) during his career, receiving 2022 honorable mention All-Big 12 Conference honors for his punt return efforts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Mims is a long-striding wideout who will primarily line up inside, but he has the potential to be moved around to mismatch speed-deficient coverage. He ran a limited route tree at Oklahoma, but he has the athletic qualities to expand on it at the next level. He’s athletic in space and dangerous with the ball in his hands, but he’s likely to see the 50/50 throws tilt in the other direction. Has can work on all three levels of the field and is an above average punt returner. Mims has just average size and strength, but his ability to create explosive plays could push him into a Day 2 selection and a starting role in the future.
strengths: Ability to line up from anywhere on the field and find catches. | Averaged 19.5 yards per catch for his career. | Long-strider with dangerous build-up speed. | Locks in focus to track and adjust to deep throws. | Smooth operator getting through his routes. | Run-after-catch ability to create first downs. | Decisive punt returner with quick downhill trigger.
weaknesses: Schemed wide open for several touchdowns during his career. | Slightly below average winning contested battles downfield. | Needs to tighten up route running underneath. | Limited catch radius to secure off-frame throws. | Will cut slants short from time to time.

bio: Pierre matriculated to Fort Scott Community College in 2018 after helping Mater Dei High School win a New Jersey Non-Public School state title as a senior. He redshirted his only season there, moving on to Butler Community College for the 2019 season (posting 42 tackles). Pierre transferred again, starting three of six games played at Murray State in the spring of 2021 (29 tackles, four for loss, one interception -- returned for a score). He transferred one more time for 2021, starting three of 14 appearances for Kent State (53 tackles, 3.5 for loss with one sack). Pierre was a standout on defense for the Golden Flashes in his final season, recording 96 tackles, 7.5 for loss with 1.5 sacks, one interception (again, returned for a touchdown), two pass breakups and two forced fumbles in 11 games with 10 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Pierre’s special teams production and explosive pro day testing could grab a team’s attention when searching for a potential special teams ace. He doesn’t make tackles consistently enough to trust as an NFL linebacker right now, but he does have pass-rush ability. He’s unlikely to be drafted but could get a look in camp as a free agent signee.
strengths: Good speed with explosive lower half. | Power in hips to play under block and hold his ground. | Possesses physical tools for man coverage. | Undeterred with good contact balance as pass rusher. | Special teams ace with 14 tackles over the last two seasons, per PFF.
weaknesses: Allows blockers to sink in and control him. | Below-average field vision and instincts. | Lacks clear-cut skill set to hang his hat on. | Broken tackles are an issue for him. | Fails to recognize route/responsibilities in coverage.

bio: Landers signed with Georgia as a three-star recruit and first-team All-Florida Class 2A selection from St. Petersburg High School. He redshirted in 2017 and then played in 25 games as a reserve over the next three years (no stats in 2018, 10-105-10.5, one TD receiving in 2019, 2-27-13.5 in 2020) before transferring to Toledo. Landers led the Golden Rockets with 25.7 yards per reception in 12 games in 2021 (20-514, five TDs) before entering the transfer portal again, returning to the SEC to play for the Razorbacks. He topped the squad with 901 receiving yards and eight scores (47 receptions, 19.2 per) while starting 12 of 13 games played. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Landers spent his first four seasons at Georgia, managing just 12 total catches before having a solid 2021 season at Toledo and then a stronger 2022 campaign at Arkansas. He’s still unrefined as a receiver, but his size, athleticism and potential as a ball-winner are noteworthy. He has legitimate build-up speed deep and his long strides help him separate. He’s a developmental prospect with upside and should hear his name called on Day 3 of the draft.
strengths: Long, athletic strides create build-up speed. | Displayed big-play ability with long touchdowns. | Clever footwork and leverage to manipulate defenders. | Uses off-hand to battle boundary bullying on outside release. | Stacks defenders quickly when he beats them. | Maintains ball-tracking focus through handsy coverage. | Outstanding height/length to elevate and win deep.
weaknesses: Struggled to win contested catches against Alabama. | Linear press release can lead to him being rerouted. | Sloppy slant routes allow coverage too much access. | Needs better physicality securing catch space underneath. | Drops arise from inconsistent catch technique. | Below-average lower body strength for run after catch.

bio: Bergeron is a Quebec native who joined Syracuse in 2019, starting five of 12 appearances at right tackle to become the first freshman to start outside for the Orange in nearly 20 years. Bergeron started all 11 games in 2020, the first three at right tackle and the final eight at left tackle. He started all 12 games on the blindside in 2021, garnering honorable mention All-ACC notice. League coaches voted him second-team all-conference for his play in 11 starts at left tackle his senior year. Bergeron opted out of the team's bowl game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A college tackle who could be best playing inside at guard, Bergeron is evenly proportioned and wears his weight well on a compact frame. He’s a dynamic run blocker, able to excel in all three phases (positioning, sustain and finish). He’s just as capable of climbing and tagging second-level linebackers as he is at opening run lanes at the point of attack with leg drive. He’s athletic enough to play tackle, but inconsistent anchor and hand placement could cause concern for evaluators. While his protection issues are potentially correctable, Bergeron’s scheme-versatile, Pro Bowl-caliber run-blocking potential might hasten a team’s decision to move him inside.
strengths: Starting experience at both tackle spots. | Shows a strong desire to impose his will on the man across from him. | Run-blocking technique is top-notch across the board. | Fits into his target with his head up and hips unlocked. | Kicks or caves his block with rapid-fire foot chop from a leveraged position. | Improves his positioning through the sustain phase of the block. | Body control and radar to make his blocks against second-level linebackers. | Quick initial slide steps to range out to speed rush. | Hips can open quickly and ride rusher up the arc. | Stays connected to rushers with quality hand latch.
weaknesses: Hand placement in pass protection is a concern. | Inconsistent footwork getting into his pass sets. | Punch can swing wide, opening his chest. | Gives far too much ground to bull-rushers. | His punch lands high and wide, which limits natural core and anchor strength. | Needs to be careful about overshooting lateral landmarks as a run blocker.

bio: Duggan was a star quarterback at Lewis Central High School, winning the 2018 Iowa Gatorade Player of the Year award and receiving four-star recruiting grades. He started 10 games for the Horned Frogs as a true freshman (181-339-53.4%, 2,077 yards, 15 TDs, 10 INTs passing; 130-555-4.3, six TDs rushing in 12 appearances). Team doctors found a heart abnormality during a standard exam in 2020 but he had surgery and returned for the season. He started nine of 10 games in 2020 (146-240-60.8%, 1,795 yards, 10 TDs, four INTs) and led TCU in rushing (116-526-4.5, 10 TDs). Duggan missed two games with a foot injury in 2021, starting 10 contests his junior campaign (145-227-63.9%, 2,048 yards, 16 TDs, six INTs passing; 105-352-3.4, three TDs rushing). He did not start the 2022 opener for TCU but took over as the starter after Chandler Morris sustained an injury in the opener. Duggan led the Horned Frogs to the College Football Playoff, throwing for 3,698 yards and 32 TDs against eight INTs (267-419-63.7%; 137-423-3.1, 9 TDs rushing). Duggan was the Big 12 Conference Offensive Player of the Year, a second-team Associated Press All-American and winner of the Davey O'Brien (named after the former TCU star) and Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Awards as the nation's top quarterback. The Heisman Trophy runner-up ranked ninth in the FBS with 4,121 total yards and tied for sixth with 41 total touchdowns. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Scrappy quarterback possessing the attitude, toughness and leadership that teams love. Duggan has proven himself to be capable of overcoming adversity and finding ways to help his team win with his arm or legs. However, he has limited arm strength and frequently forces receivers to break stride on deep balls and crossing routes. Duggan’s intangibles give him a chance to become an NFL backup but his limitations as a passer cap his ceiling.
strengths: Displays physical and mental toughness. | Finds a comfortable passing rhythm from RPOs. | Resolute runner with 28 career rushing touchdowns. | Ability to scan through progressions. | Slides inside and outside the pocket to extend the play. | Showed ability to hang in and beat the blitz against Michigan. | Improvisational thrower with compact release. | Unafraid to challenge safeties when a good opportunity arises.
weaknesses: Below average size and play traits. | Stares down target, allowing safeties to read and range. | Threw into congestion when better options were available. | Frequently forced receivers to break stride. | Below average deep-ball power and placement. | Nose of the ball dives on long, field-side throws.

bio: Smith was a four-star, top-50 recruit and a two-time all-state pick at East Kentwood High School in Michigan before arriving in Ann Arbor. He played in two games during his redshirt season (no statistics) and then in five contests off the bench in 2020 (three tackles, one for loss). Smith started all 14 games in 2021, garnering honorable mention All-Big Ten Conference notice (37 tackles, 2.5 for loss, four pass breakups). He was a first-team All-Big Ten pick in 2022 (48 tackles, 2.5 for loss in 14 starts). In October, he was stopped by police for speeding and was arrested for possessing a concealed weapon without a valid license to carry one. Smith later told reporters he was in the process of completing the paperwork to acquire the proper permit when he was stopped by police. He pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor and was sentenced to probation. Smith's grandfather, Carl, started a Black freedom movement newspaper called "The Organizer" in the 1960s and eventually worked for the Michigan Department of Civil Rights. His mother's first cousin, Sekou Smith, was a long-time ESPN NBA writer before passing away in 2021. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Dontari Poe might be the physical and athletic player comparison for Smith, but more consistency from Smith is needed before he finds the Pro Bowl, as Poe did twice in his career. Smith’s blend of size and quickness is rare. He can punch and control a base block with relative ease. However, he struggles to match the initial movement of move blockers, which diminishes his effectiveness. He has space-eating potential but needs to become more consistent at taking on double teams and securing his gap. Smith’s size and testing could give his draft slotting some juice but he’s more of a Day 2 talent with exciting upside than a plug-and-play starter.
strengths: Possesses rare combination of size and athleticism. | Bendy and stout in his lower half. | Power to punch and lift blocker under his pads. | Plays with lively feet and short-area quickness. | Able to slide, swim and seize the gap. | Yanks and pulls guards off-balance from any direction. | Foot quickness to be part of a twisting rush unit.
weaknesses: Hasn’t made many plays behind the line of scrimmage. | Motor runs out of gas when tempo heats up. | Slow reaction to movement gets him sealed. | Struggled against Iowa’s zone scheme attack. | Surprising lack of anchor consistency against double teams. | Unlikely to see many passing downs as a pro.

bio: The former three-star recruit played in 10 games as a reserve in his redshirt freshman season with the Moccs before starting all 12 games (11 at right guard, one at left guard) in 2019. He garnered first-team All-Southern Conference honors in 2020 (started four games at right guard) and 2021 (started all 11 games at right guard). Curtis' play and increased visibility allowed him to earn second-team Associated Press All-American honors as well as the SoCon Jacobs Blocking Trophy as the conference's top lineman. He started 11 games in this third consecutive first-team All-SoCon campaign, with the first four at right guard and the final seven at left tackle -- even playing both positions in multiple games. Curtis was also a two-time finalist for the FedEx Ground Doris Robinson Scholar-Athlete Award. -- Chad Reuter
overview: Guard prospect with the build of a long-armed offensive tackle. Despite his traits, Curtis has too many holes in his game to trust he will be ready to step up in competition early on. His struggles in trying to separate and sustain against Illinois’ interior defenders really shined a bright light on the work he needs to do to get stronger and more technically sound. Despite these concerns, Curtis is capable in pocket protection and is likely to be viewed as a Day 3 prospect requiring a plan and coaching to help him develop.
strengths: Broad frame with good muscle mass. | Size and length allow for two-gap control in pass pro. | Able to redirect B-gap rushers away from pocket. | Always looking to help his friends when uncovered on pass plays. | Works to steer defenders with inside hand on zone blocks.
weaknesses: Tape from Illinois game was troubling. | Run blocks with excessive forward lean, diminishing his balance. | Needs to upgrade upper-body strength as a run blocker. | Lacks ideal coordination to move and strike with fluidity. | Stronger interior challengers play through his inside edge to capture the gap. | Gets too straight-legged through contact in pass pro.

bio: Blackmon grew up in the hometown of NFL star Davante Adams, playing on the same AAU basketball team Adams did, albeit a few years after the receiver. The honorable mention All-San Francisco Metro pick as a senior at Menlo-Atherton High School began his collegiate career at the College of San Mateo. After one year there, he transferred to Colorado for the 2018 season, when he started three of eight appearances (10 tackles, two pass breakups). Blackmon redshirted in 2019, however, after trying to play through a shoulder injury for four games (10 tackles, two starts). He started all six of the Buffaloes' games in 2020, making 15 tackles, intercepting one pass and breaking up six others. Blackmon missed three games due to injury in 2021 but still garnered honorable mention All-Pac-12 honors by starting eight of nine games played (41 tackles, one interception, four pass breakups). He returned to California for his final season, heading to Los Angeles to play for the Trojans, and he garnered third-team AP All-American and first-team all-conference honors after intercepting three passes, breaking up a team-high 12 passes and posting 66 tackles in 14 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Aggressive man-cover cornerback whose physical play brings both passes defensed and penalties. Blackmon gives receivers a rough ride over the first five yards, but his extended grabbing will be less tolerated by NFL officials. He’s capable of phasing routes when matching from press, but he doesn’t have the hips to transition smoothly when playing off-man coverage. He’s talented at squeezing the catch space and timing his challenges, but Blackmon’s lack of size and fluidity could limit his pro chances.
strengths: Has experience playing outside and in the slot. | Fires quick, accurate strikes into opponent's chest from press. | Stays in phase and squeezes tight to the route. | Consistent finding positioning when recovering or transitioning. | Tracks and adjusts to deep throws like a wide receiver. | Well-timed leaps help him get to high point.
weaknesses: Too tight-hipped to swivel freely and shadow route breaks. | Needs multiple gather steps to plant and go from his pedal. | Relies on grab-and-pull defense at the top of the route. | Could become an illegal-contact machine. | Big bodies will overtake him on jump balls. | Below-average play strength as a tackle finisher.

bio: Garner began his collegiate career at Navarro College in 2018, intercepting two passes, breaking up five others and making 48 tackles in 10 games. The graduate of Poteet High School in Texas transferred to Louisiana for 2019, redshirting that season but playing in two contests (four tackles). He started eight of 11 games played in 2020, garnering honorable mention All-Sun Belt Conference honors (27 tackles, one sack, three interceptions, seven pass breakups). Garner was a third-team all-conference selection as a junior (31 tackles, 2.5 for loss, eight pass breakups) in 13 games with 11 starts before entering the transfer portal. He started 13 games for LSU in 2022, tying for the team lead with eight pass breakups to go along with 43 tackles (1.5 for loss) before opting out of the team's bowl game to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Garner is a big, long corner with a jarring press. However, he’s missing the footwork and body control to phase and match NFL routes that force him to change direction. He’s a handful when he’s in position to challenge the throw, but teams might need to plug him into a Cover 2 scheme or try him at safety, where he can help support the run and cover tight ends.
strengths: Big, strong and long as a defensive back. | Press punch can put receiver in neutral. | Able to track and adjust downfield from lateral shuffle. | Physically overwhelms receivers when contesting. | Punishing hitter from zone. | Able to play past or off of blocks and turn runs back inside.
weaknesses: No interceptions over the last two seasons. | Below-average footwork adjusting to receiver’s release. | Lacks necessary balance for pattern matching in space. | Short-area quickness and top-end speed are below par. | Top-heavy and sluggish to change direction and hit the accelerator. | Might need to upgrade tackle consistency if he moves to safety.

bio: The four-star recruit jumped into the fray immediately, playing eight games with one start as a true freshman (18 tackles). Baskerville played in 12 games as a reserve for the 2019 national champions (15 tackles, four for loss, with one sack) and then started seven of eight contests in 2020 to help replace Jacob Phillips and Patrick Queen (55 tackles, 4.5 for loss). He missed 2021 spring practices because of academic issues but returned to start 12 games in the fall, setting career highs with 83 tackles, nine for loss with two sacks, one interception and three pass breakups. Baskerville sat out the team's bowl game for undisclosed reasons but returned for 2022, leading the Tigers with 89 tackles (4.5 for loss with one sack), intercepting one pass and breaking up a team-high eight others in 14 appearances (10 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Inside/outside linebacker prospect who falls short from a measurables standpoint but understands the game. Baskerville needs more strength, is a limited athlete and can be overtaken by blockers at times, but he plays with excellent pre- and post-snap recognition that leads him to the action. His football IQ and special teams background are important boxes for him to check, but he needs to test well to give himself a good chance of earning a roster spot.
strengths: Experience as inside and outside linebacker. | Very instinctive and plays with a high football IQ. | Offensive alignment alerts his play anticipation. | Identifies his keys and clues to arrive at designed run lane. | Good balance between route development and QB’s eyes. | Core special teams performer at LSU.
weaknesses: Will need to improve play strength as a pro. | Can be mauled by blockers on second level. | Inconsistent leveraging his gap. | Build-up runner who is slow to accelerate in pursuit. | Below-average athlete in space. | Can be exploited if forced to cover running backs.

bio: A first-team All-Ohio selection in football and three-time city champion wrestler from Walnut Ridge High School, Ayers signed with Ashland for the 2017 season. He started nine times in 2018 as a redshirt freshman (23 tackles, 3.5 for loss with two sacks, two pass breakups in 10 games) and 2019 (27 tackles, 2.5 for loss, one interception in 11 games). The school did not play in 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns, but Ayers made the most of the sport's return in 2021, winning the Great Midwest Athletic Conference Defensive Player of the Year Award and leading the team with 100 tackles, 12 for loss (with three sacks) and two forced fumbles in 10 starts. The two-time first-team All-GMAC selection was the conference player of the year in his final college season (team-high 81 tackles, 10.5 tackles for loss, three sacks, eight pass breakups and three forced fumbles in 12 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: As a safety turned linebacker, Ayers has a legitimate chance of competing for a spot on a practice squad or maybe even a roster. He needs to get stronger and fails to stand out with his speed, but he offers versatility thanks to his coverage background and ability to rush the passer. Provided he improves his strength and proves he can handle special teams assignments, Ayers could have a future as a backup 4-3 outside linebacker.
strengths: Added close to 40 pounds of good weight since arriving at Ashland. | Posted 28.5 tackles for loss and six forced fumbles during his college career. | Sees block development and run-lane choices from runners. | Fluid when sinking and transitioning in coverage. | Brings experience as a rusher off the edge.
weaknesses: Will need to get bigger and stronger for the pro game. | Needs to improve as a block-slipper near the line of scrimmage. | Can be turned and eliminated from the play by climbing blockers. | Speed is average as an outside linebacker.

bio: Ezeike stayed in California to play for the Bruins after being ranked among the top 10 tight end recruits in the country out of Colony High School. He started off at receiver, though, starting twice in 10 games as a true freshman (12-136-11.3, two TDs). Ezeike did not have a catch the following two seasons and then moved to tight end for the 2021 season (3-45-15.0, one TD in 12 games, one start). He set career highs with 20 receptions for 226 yards (11.3 per) and four touchdowns in 12 games with eight starts in 2022. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Former wideout who is continuing to grow into his frame as a tight end. Ezeike lacks poise and body control getting into his blocks, but once’s he there, he displays some fight and hand strength to maintain the battle. He’s not very elusive as a route runner, but he does show decent talent after the catch. He’s a developmental prospect, but he could find his way onto a practice squad.
strengths: Added around 30 pounds since the start of his UCLA career. | Puts decent effort into blocking with room for improvement. | Latches in with hand strength for improved block sustain. | Build-up speed on intermediate routes. | Good stiff-arm and physicality as a run-finisher after the catch.
weaknesses: Enters blocks with elevated pad level and outside hands. | Lacks body control needed for consistent run blocking. | Below-average hand quickness as pass-catcher. | Sluggish into routes and uncovering underneath.

bio: Jefferson signed with Alabama State for 2018, making 11 catches for 91 yards and four touchdowns as a true freshman. He led the Hornets in receiving the following year (49-767-15.7), tying the school record with 12 receiving scores, and started all five games of the team's 2021 spring season (24-234-9.8, two TDs) as the team did not play in the fall due to COVID-19 concerns. Jefferson transferred to Louisiana for 2021, earning honorable mention All-Sun Belt honors as a big-play receiver (18-481-26.7, four TDs). He was a third-team pick in 2022, starting 12 games and again leading the team in receiving (51-810-15.9, seven TDs). Jefferson opted out of the Independence Bowl to prepare for the draft. Jefferson was involved in an April 9 car accident in Alabama in which a 55-year-old man was killed. In an April 20 statement to The Associated Press, Jefferson’s attorney, Brad Sohn, said Jefferson "still has optimism that -- even as he continues to undergo grueling rehabilitation -- he can have an outstanding NFL career." -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Jefferson is a tall target with build-up speed and a receiving style that gets better the further he gets from the line. He doesn’t have the short-area quickness to elude NFL press effectively and could struggle to uncover against tight man coverage over the first two levels. He has decent ball skills and works into the zones effectively, but he will have a challenging time making an NFL roster.
strengths: Impressive touchdown-to-catch ratio. | Runs routes with good patience and to completion. | Long, smooth strides create quiet build-up speed. | Sells downfield stems with exaggerated hip fakes. | Quicker gather-and-turn than expected on comebacks. | Above-average win-in-air potential.
weaknesses: Takes too long getting feet engaged to beat press. | Getting away from man coverage could be challenging. | Dropped deep passes that should have been catches in 2022. | Below-average plant-and-turn quickness underneath. | Requires a linear-specific route tree.

bio: Mayer had his eye on a college basketball scholarship when he entered Covington Catholic High School in Independence, Kentucky, but was convinced to give football a shot, joining his quarterback brother, A.J. He was named the state's Gatorade Player of the Year as a senior (catching 15 TDs and picking off four INTs), helping his school win a state title. Mayer's Notre Dame career started with a bang, as he garnered Freshman All-American and third-team All-ACC honors by tying for the Irish lead with 42 receptions (450 yards, 10.7 per, two TDs in 12 games, three starts). He again topped the squad with 71 receptions (840 yards, 11.8 per) and tied for the team lead with seven receiving scores in 12 starts his sophomore campaign. Mayer was a first-team Associated Press All-American and John Mackey Award (nation's top tight end) finalist his junior season, breaking his own school record for tight ends with nine receiving touchdowns and leading the team with 67 receptions for 809 receiving yards (12.1 per). He also set the Notre Dame record for tight ends in single-season receptions and receiving yards in 2021 and is the school's all-time leader in all three categories for the position. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Big combination tight end with the demeanor for run blocking and the size for tough, chain-moving catches underneath. Mayer will come into the league with better blocking technique than most tight ends in this year’s draft. He’s built for in-line duty and was an extension of the Notre Dame offensive line at times. His feet are a little heavy getting into and through his routes, but he has the hand strength and contact balance to win heavily contested catches on the first two levels. Mayer might need to polish his route running to become a high-volume target, but he’s a safe pick and will be a good pro who can become a plus player as a run blocker and pass catcher.
strengths: Possesses ideal frame and demeanor to play Y tight end in the NFL. | Makes effort to strain and win his run blocks. | Meets defender with foot slide to gain positioning. | Fits up his run blocks with decent force. | Can climb on top of defender’s toes before snapping break off. | Maintains his stride speed through route turns. | Rarely distracted by route or catch conflict. | Sinks suddenly into zone void and presents numbers to his quarterback. | Plays big when it’s time to win the contested catch.
weaknesses: Needs to get into blocks with quicker hands. | Sluggish release and acceleration off the line. | Won’t generate much separation at stems and turns. | Occasional slips getting out of breaks underneath. | Likely to see heavier contested catch totals at the next level. | Upper body looks a little tight when reaching outside the frame to catch. | Below average run-after-catch talent.

bio: Turk is the nephew of 19-year NFL punting veteran Matt Turk and pro offensive lineman/long snapper Dan Turk, who passed away in 2000 from cancer. He began his college career at FCS school Lafayette, where he garnered second-team All-Patriot League honors in 2017 by averaging 42.7 yards per punt (67-2,862), placing 18 of 67 kicks inside the 20-yard line against just three touchbacks, and forcing 15 fair catches. Turk decided to transfer to ASU after that season, meaning he would have to sit out the fall of 2018, per NCAA regulations. He excelled in his first season with the Sun Devils, leading the Pac-12 in punting average (67-3,082-46.0) to receive first-team all-conference recognition. He forced fair catches on 22 of 67 punts, putting 36 of those kicks inside the 20 with seven touchbacks. Turk entered the 2020 draft and set a modern era record for punters with 25 bench-press reps at the NFL Scouting Combine. He went undrafted and was granted a special waiver by the NCAA to regain his college eligibility. He earned first-team All-Pac-12 notice again in 2020 by averaging 47.2 yards per punt (six inside the 20, two fair catches on 14 punts, four touchbacks). Turk transferred to Oklahoma for 2021, where he was awarded first-team All-Big 12 Conference honors and averaged 51.2 yards per punt, which would have ranked second in the FBS but he did not have enough attempts to qualify (35-1,791, eight fair catches, 16 inside the 20 against four touchbacks). Turk was a first-team all-league selection in 2022, ranking third in the FBS in gross punt average (63-2,948-46.8, 24 fair catches, 22 inside the 20 against 10 touchbacks). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Like a home run hitter in baseball, Turk has tremendous power but is lacking ball control to plant opposing teams against their end zone instead of kicking for touchbacks. He has improved his hang-time and outkicked his coverage a little less frequently, which will matter for NFL evaluators. The pure power and talent could get him a Day 3 look.
strengths: Very thickly muscled. | Has experience training with uncle and former NFL punter, Matt Turk. | Powerful leg to flip the field when needed. | Had a punt of 50-plus yards in 11 of 13 games in 2022. | Good operation quickness and hang-time.
weaknesses: Has had issues outkicking coverage and allowing returns. | Lacks touch on pooch punts, sending too many into the end zone. | Inconsistent control as directional punter.

bio: The former four-star recruit from Chaminade High School in Southern California matriculated north for 2018, playing in all 13 games as a true freshman with two starts (14-126-9.0, one TD receiving: 8-65-8.1 punt returns). Wilson started all 12 games in 2019, leading the Cardinal in receiving (56-672-12.0, five TDs; also 12-72-6.0 punt returns). He missed the end of the 2020 season with a foot injury but still garnered honorable mention All-Pac-12 notice from league coaches for his work in four starts (19-261-13.7, one TD receiving; 2-14-7.0 punt returns). Wilson returned to start the team's final four games in 2021 (19-185-9.7) but then missed the second half of the 2022 season with an injury (26-418-16.1, four TDs in six starts). Again, Pac-12 coaches voted him to the honorable mention rolls even though he missed time. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Energetic wideout who plays the game with excellent urgency and effort. Wilson plays to his top speed at all times, but he needs to become a more efficient route runner to beat NFL coverage. The ball skills are a little below average, but he’s a cantankerous run blocker and has the potential to become a very good gunner on special teams. Staying healthy will be priority No. 1 for Wilson, but his versatility and competitive nature should give him a chance to become a plus NFL backup with upside.
strengths: Voted team captain. | Plays the game with tangible urgency. | Experienced with more complicated route asks. | Creates early separation with long strides. | Runs with good toughness after the catch. | Eager and effective as a run blocker. | Gets into opposition with positioning and pop. | Above-average talent and traits for role as a gunner on special teams.
weaknesses: Has played in just 14 games over the last three seasons. | Held up too easily by press coverage. | Excessive wasted motion into the top of the route. | Leaner who occasionally slips out of route breaks. | Lacks natural ball skills down the field. | Needs to carve out cleaner catch space underneath. | Can be a tick late to get his hands catch-ready.

bio: Morris nearly followed in his father's footsteps to play at Florida State; Mike Morris Sr. was an offensive lineman for FSU when it beat the Wolverines at home in 1991. The four-star recruit from American Heritage High School flipped to Michigan to make his own path, however, though it took a couple of seasons. Morris redshirted in 2019 and played in one game (one tackle) the next season. He began fulfilling his promise with four starts in 14 appearances in 2021 (16 tackles, one for loss, one interception). Morris was named Big Ten Conference Defensive Lineman of the Year in 2022, leading the Wolverines with 11 tackles for loss, including 7.5 sacks, among 23 total stops (also posting three pass breakups, one blocked kick and one forced fumbles) in 12 games with 11 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: We won’t dismiss the production, size or the athleticism Morris shows on tape, but his disappointing NFL Scouting Combine testing should force teams to reevaluate him. He needs to crank up his intensity on a more regular basis, but his ability to take on blockers and create advantages flashes in every game. His run defense will trend ahead of the pass rush until he becomes more skilled with his hands and at creating angles of entry. Morris could have the versatility to play in odd or even fronts, but it might take a couple of years for him to hit his stride.
strengths: Traits for consideration in both 4-3 and 3-4 schemes. | Tailor-made for end/tackle twists. | Stab-and-swim rush move is beginning to blossom. | Impressive blend of power and change of direction. | Punches and sinks a deep anchor when setting the edge. | Uses length and lower-body power to cross-face the tackle. | Flies in to stop runner in back-side pursuit.
weaknesses: Still working on finding his hands and go-to moves as rusher. | Rides on blocks too often when rush stalls. | Needs better pad level to generate pocket push. | Hands lack violence to batter the tackle’s punch. | Motor and aggression are lukewarm at times. | Very average at attacking and stacking pulling blockers. | Disappointing tackle production (37 in his career) relative to his gifts.

bio: Jones played two seasons at IMG Academy in Florida, catching the eye of Syracuse's coaching staff. They started him four times his true freshman year (38 tackles, two for loss in 12 appearances) and then gave him the reins to the defense in 2020, when he garnered honorable mention All-ACC honors with a team-high 69 tackles (two for loss with one sack) and four interceptions (also forcing three fumbles) in 11 starts. Jones was a first-team all-conference pick in 2021, topping the Orange with 110 tackles and 13 tackles for loss (with four sacks) in 12 starts. He was a third-team selection as a senior (84 tackles, seven for loss with four sacks), starting 11 games before missing the end of the regular season with an injury and then opting out of the team's bowl game. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Team leader who plays bigger than his listed size. Jones has plenty of toughness and thump behind his pads, but getting off of blocks and making plays against NFL quickness could be too much for Jones to handle. He lacks fluidity and twitch. The game will get tougher for him when it’s not played inside the tackle box.
strengths: Three-year starter and two-time team captain. | Keeps eyes past blockers and on ball-carriers. | Stays wide and ready to slip the block while reading play. | Tackles with heavy pads and finishes. | Natural rush instincts when called on as blitzer.
weaknesses: Below-average size and frame for inside linebacker. | Hip tightness limits short-area reactions. | Allows blockers to get too far into his frame. | Below-average chase speed when plays flow wide. | Will have trouble staying with man coverage.

bio: Tinsley only played one year of high school football before signing with Hutchinson Community College for the 2018 season. He played well enough as a sophomore to earn a scholarship to Western Kentucky, where he led the Hilltoppers in receiving in 2020 (43-377, four TDs in 12 games, nine starts). Tinsley's production skyrocketed in 14 starts with quarterback Bailey Zappe leading a prolific offense in 2021, garnering second-team All-Conference USA honors and ranking fifth in the FBS with 14 receiving scores and eighth with 1,402 receiving yards (87 receptions, 16.1 per). Tinsley transferred to Penn State for 2022, starting nine of 13 appearances (51-577-11.3, five TDs receiving; 4-4-1.0 punt returns). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Possession receiver lacking top-end speed and separation quickness but possessing quality ball skills. Tinsley’s lack of suddenness shows up quickly in press release and when trying to separate early in the route, but he’s very willing in the middle of the field and has terrific ball skills. He has the focus to make challenging catches at any spot on the field. He has good size and is a gamer, but a lack of athletic features might require him to play the role of zone-beater from the slot.
strengths: Possesses NFL frame and has big hands. | Has the physicality to create breathing room at top of the route. | Big-time focus intensity when ball goes up. | Able to track and bring throws in over the shoulder. | Ignores distractions and catches in traffic. | Puts in his work when asked to block in run game.
weaknesses: Lacks foot quickness to elude quality press-man. | Upright, high-stepping stride gives away impending break. | Below-average short-area suddenness to uncover in tight quarters. | Monotonous route tempo lacks juice. | Heavy feet with a lack of burst out of stems and turns.

bio: Ibrahim matriculated from Baltimore to Minnesota in 2017. He redshirted his first year with the Gophers before starting nine of 10 games in 2018, garnering honorable mention All-Big Ten honors (202-1,160-5.7, nine TDs rushing; 4-26-6.5 receiving) despite missing three games due to injury. Ibrahim played in 11 games as a reserve in 2019 (114-604-5.3, seven TDs rushing; 3-13-4.3 receiving). In 2020, he ranked among the top 10 in the FBS with 15 rushing touchdowns (201-1,076-5.4 rushing: 8-56-7.0 receiving in seven starts) to earn third-team Associated Press All-American and first-team all-conference accolades. Ibrahim suffered a ruptured Achilles in the 2021 opener (30-163-5.4, two TDs) and missed the rest of the season. He returned in 2022, grabbing second-team Associated Press All-American and first-team All-Big Ten accolades by setting school records with 320 carries for 1,665 rushing yards (5.2 per; also 7-50-7.1 receiving) and tying for the FBS lead with 20 rushing touchdowns in 12 starts. Ibrahim also set the Minnesota career rushing yardage (4,668) and rushing touchdown (53) records. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Hard-hat running back who operated with toughness, vision and a feel for cut timing in the Minnesota inside/outside zone attack. Ibrahim’s decisiveness stands out, but he’s missing an elevated burst to clear second-level tacklers without taking bumps and bruises. He’s not going to run away from NFL defenders, so creativity will be important to keep runs alive. His injury history, paired with his combative running style, could be a concern for some teams, but his no-nonsense running approach and innate feel for the end zone will be easy for coaches to love.
strengths: Adequate size with compact frame and low center of gravity. | Patient waiting for his blocks, but decisive when they come. | Efficient in reading the run lane development. | Absorbs contact with squared pads and a balanced base. | Hits like a hammer when finishing his runs. | Talented short yardage back with the ability to find small crevices. | Punched in 37 rushing touchdowns over his last 20 games. | Rarely used as receiver but has hands to catch out of the backfield.
weaknesses: Missing threatening speed flowing wide. | Average burst forces him into a role of grinder. | Not enough creativity to elude early traffic consistently. | Missed all but one game of the 2021 season with Achilles tear. | Sidelined by injury for at least one game in four of the past five seasons.

bio: Mohamoud Diabate (pronounced MAH-mood DEE-ah-BAH-tay) was a first-team All-Alabama pick his senior year at Auburn High School and signed with Florida. He started one contest as a true freshman in Gainesville (18 tackles, 4.5 sacks in 13 games played) and six times as a sophomore (69 tackles, seven for loss with 1.5 sacks, one interception in 12 games). Diabate started 10 of 12 appearances in 2021 (89 tackles, 2.5 for loss) but entered the transfer portal after the season. He moved on to Utah after having shoulder surgery. Diabate started 12 games, missing two due to injury, and led the Utes with 13.5 tackles for loss (with five sacks among 58 total tackles). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Diabate is a physical tackler with a pretty good feel for sifting through the trash to find the ball between the tackles. However, when plays flow wide or he needs to play with agility and pursuit speed, the level of play consistency can take a tumble. The instincts and recognition are just average and he's a better rusher than cover man against the pass. Diabate has an outside shot of competing for a roster spot.
strengths: Nearly a quarter of his tackles in 2022 were for a loss. | Keys linemen to help flow to the rendezvous point. | Good toughness at the point of impact as a hitter. | Runs his feet all the way through his target to finish. | Adequate patience and vision sifting through blockers. | Displayed talent to slip through gaps as blitzer.
weaknesses: Plays upright and straight-legged in space. | Lacks fluidity and pace flowing laterally with the run. | Slowed noticeably by misdirection in the running game. | Side-steps blocks, losing gap leverage as run defender. | Loses sight of coverage duties against play fakes. | Below-average athleticism when asked to cover in space.

bio: Braswell signed with Central Michigan after earning second-team All-Florida honors as a senior at Avon Park High School. As a redshirt freshman with the Chippewas, he tied for the team lead with 10 pass breakups while starting six of 14 appearances (34 tackles, one interception; 13-289-22.2 kick returns). Braswell entered the transfer portal after the season and signed with Missouri State. The Bears did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns. He was a first-team All-Missouri Valley Football Conference selection in the spring of 2021 (41 tackles, three interceptions -- one returned for a score -- four pass breakups in seven starts; 8-233-29.1, one TD kick returns). Braswell was a second-team Associated Press All-American and first-team all-conference pick in 2021, ranking seventh in the FCS with 1.42 passes defensed per game (four interceptions, 13 pass breakups in 12 starts) and also ranked fifth in the FCS with 29.5 yards per kick return (20-589, one TD). He was a first-team All-MVFC pick as a cornerback (44 tackles, three pass breakups) and returner in 2022 (12-364-30.3, one TD kick returns). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Braswell lacks great top-end speed and outstanding testing numbers. He has average size for a perimeter cornerback, but it appears he shows way too much respect to the opposition, allowing unnecessary catch space. His ball production has been good in the past and he’s a very talented kick returner with big-play ability in that department. He needs to become a more consistent cornerback if he wants to make a team.
strengths: Tracks the deep ball effectively.* Crowds receiver and competes downfield.* Impressive overall ball production in college.* Tape from 2021 might be a better watch to gauge his potential.* Dangerous kickoff returner with three career touchdowns.
weaknesses: Below-average short-area agility.* Allows too much space pre- and post-route breaks.* Has trouble making up distance when he falls behind.* Very inconsistent use of leverage near the goal line.* Run support will be a concern.

bio: Ojomo was born in Nigeria and moved to the United States when he was 7 years old. He became a second-team all-state pick as a senior at Katy High School. He played in three games off the bench (no statistics) during his redshirt season at Texas. Ojomo played in all 13 games in 2019, starting twice (13 tackles, 2.5 for loss) before getting the nod to begin all 10 games of the 2020 campaign (21 tackles, 2.5 for loss with two sacks). Big 12 coaches voted him honorable mention all-conference in 2021 (29 tackles, three for loss, 12 starts) and 2022 (32 tackles, 5.5 for loss with three sacks in 12 games, five starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Naturally powerful defensive lineman caught somewhere between end and tackle. Ojomo is best-suited as a base end but doesn’t really have the get-off quickness to exploit interior blockers as an inside rusher on passing downs. He’s tight in his lower body, and his movements lack fluidity, but he can fight his way through blocks with upper-body power and a will to make it happen. Ojomo plays hard throughout the rep and will find production with his secondary effort, but he might cap out as a solid backup in either an odd or even front.
strengths: Three-year starter. | Forces his way across the face of back-side blocks. | Lower-body strength to plow through a blocker’s edge. | Consistent in rallying to the football until whistle blows. | Uses upper-body power to shove protection off-balance. | Active hands help dislodge blocker’s punch from frame. | Counters with force, creating opportunities with secondary rush.
weaknesses: Movements are mechanical and segmented. | Hip tightness limits proper pad level. | Feet are heavy when forced to slide laterally. | Needs to improve technique to play in odd fronts. | Lacking edge-to-edge foot quickness in his rush. | Below-average snap quickness as interior rusher.

bio: Brooks committed to Arkansas out of Hendrickson High School in Pflugerville, Texas, but wound up staying closer to home and playing at Stephen F. Austin. As a true freshman in 2019, he started three of 10 games played (23 tackles, one interception, six pass breakups), before starting four of nine appearances in the shortened 2020 campaign (17 tackles, one interception, five pass breakups). Jones was a first-team All-Western Athletic Conference selection for the Lumberjacks in 2021, tying for the team lead with four interceptions (returning one for a TD) while also recording 25 tackles and six pass breakups in 12 starts. He transferred from SFA to Louisiana Tech as a senior and earned second-team All-Conference USA notice after pacing the squad with nine pass breakups and making 29 tackles, three for loss and three INTs in 12 games with 10 starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A perimeter man corner with good size and instincts, Brooks will need to prove he can continue his on-ball production against better competition. He will need to tighten up his technique, but he has the feet and feel to play press. Also, he does a nice job of competing against the route and fighting for positioning when the ball goes up. He has plus ball skills and innate timing to make plays on the throw but might need to prove his top-end speed in testing. He will have occasional issues with downfield penalties and is a below-average run defender, but he has the talent to work his way onto an NFL roster.
strengths: Possesses an NFL frame ready for press. | Patience to pedal and shuffle with tempo of the release. | Posted 12 passes defensed, including three interceptions, in 2022. | Maintains feel for vertical work and competes for space. | Finds positioning to locate the football. | Leaps and takes the ball away at its highest point. | Impressive hand timing to deflect the football at the catch point.
weaknesses: Plays a little too upright when matching release from press. | Ready to take too big of a bite out of play fakes. | Coverage can become a little loose at the top of the route. | Average top-end speed when forced into recovery. | Looks much less comfortable working zone coverages. | Loses contain and can be outflanked in run support.

bio: Murphy attended Hillgrove High School in Georgia, the same school that produced NFL players like Bradley Chubb, Kenyan Drake and Evan Engram. The top-five national prospect burst onto the scene in his first year in Death Valley, earning Freshman All-American notice with a team-high 12 tackles for loss (with four sacks among 41 total stops in 12 games, six starts). Murphy again led the Tigers with 14 tackles for loss and seven sacks in 2021 (38 tackles, two pass breakups, two forced fumbles in 13 games, 10 starts) to garner second-team All-ACC accolades. He earned first-team honors in 2022 by tying for the team lead with 6.5 sacks (among 40 total tackles, 11 for loss, two pass breakups) in 13 games with 11 starts. Myles' father, Willard, played football at Chattanooga. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Murphy has excellent size/traits and has been consistently productive in impact categories for three straight years. He plays with a plus motor and good first-step quickness, but his game isn’t really twitchy or explosive. He has finishing talent when he’s inside the pocket, but he needs to vary his rush angles and find an effective inside counter, as NFL tackles will be expecting his long-arm bull-rush technique. Murphy’s length and post-up strength could provide the scheme and positional versatility that puts him on every draft board. The traits and upside are there, but his skill level needs a boost to push the ceiling higher.
strengths: NFL size and length for scheme versatility. | Gets up the rush track with sudden first step. | Long-arm rush move to run tackle into the pocket. | Quick to recalibrate his rush after taking an early punch. | Uses long strides to escape block redirection around the rush arc. | Lateral burst to beat tackles across their face off the snap. | Slants into gaps with proper bend and leverage to counter wash-down attempts. | Uses spin move to disengage from run blocks. | Crashes down hard to spoil the run from back side. | Keeps his tank full of gas for pursuit.
weaknesses: Doesn’t come up with much of a rush plan to beat tackles. | Rides on pass blocks beyond depth of the pocket. | Needs to work on adding an inside counter to his bag. | Leggy movements can slow momentum as a rusher. | Average body control through contact. | Below average short-area agility as tackler. | Takes him time getting to top speed in pursuit.

bio: Jensen redshirted in 2017 while watching NDSU win the first of four FCS titles during his six years in Fargo. He was a backup lineman and special-teamer in 15 games in 2018 and then coaches inserted Jensen into the starting lineup at left guard for all 16 games of the 2019 campaign. He stayed at that spot for 10 games in 2020, 15 games in 2021 and 14 games in 2022 -- setting a NCAA All-Division record with 70 total games played during his career. Jensen was named a first-team Associated Press FCS All-American and first-team All-Missouri Valley Football Conference in his final season. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Jensen is a well-schooled, highly experienced guard prospect with a broad frame and above-average toughness. He hasn’t faced much NFL-caliber competition, but he displays some of the same characteristics found in pro guards. He’s below average as an athlete, but good enough for schemes that don’t rely heavily on movement in space for interior blockers. He’s not going to uproot defenders as a drive blocker, but he can work with adequate success on double teams. Jensen’s pass protection is a little more consistent than his run blocking, but athletic rushers will be a challenge for him.
strengths: Played in 70 games during North Dakota State career, making 55 starts at left guard. | Proven to be very durable and consistent. | Broadens his strike zone as base blocker. | Determined demeanor when fighting through engagement. | Pass sets with proper balance and width. | Works with independent hands to stay in the battle.
weaknesses: Small delay when changing direction in pass slides. | Lacks desired range when he’s asked to block on an island. | Below-average lateral quickness for lateral blocking asks. | Loses potential leverage due to hand placement. | Fails to keep feet rolling through first contact in run game.

bio: Adkins starred at Bearden High School in Tennessee before signing with East Tennessee State for 2018, when he started twice in 12 appearances (5-50-10.0, one TD). He built on that campaign to garner first-team All-Southern Conference recognition the next two seasons, starting 11 of 12 games played in 2019 (25-241-9.6, two TDs) and four of six contests in the spring of 2021 (10-101-10.1). The team did not play in the fall of 2020 due to COVID-19 concerns. Adkins was a second-team All-SoCon pick in 2021 (33-357-10.8, one TD) before deciding to transfer to South Carolina for his final season. He played in 13 games with nine starts in 2022, making 13 catches for 168 yards (12.9 per). His father, Greg, is an analyst for the Gamecocks. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Adkins offers good play strength and tenacity as a point-of-attack blocker. He will need to improve his hand usage and play with better consistency to adjust on the move as a lead blocker. He will catch what is thrown to him and should be able to handle every phase of special teams. Adkins might go undrafted, but he has the toughness, frame and demeanor to warrant camp consideration as an NFL fullback.
strengths: Thick, muscular frame. | Gets into his blocks with patience and balance. | Sustains with proper base width. | Works angles and looks to finish his run blocks. | Has potential to be a four-phase special-teams talent.
weaknesses: Average foot quickness adjusting to movement. | Hand placement is a little sloppy. | Slow getting in and out of breaks as a receiver.

bio: Silvera, a Miami-area native, signed with the Hurricanes as a top-50 overall recruit and two-time state champ with American Heritage High School. Silvera played in 10 games as a reserve (13 tackles, 1.5 for loss) in 2018. A foot injury limited him in 2019, when he made 19 tackles with one sack coming off the bench for the final nine games. He bounced back in 2020, however, garnering honorable mention All-ACC notice (35 tackles, eight for loss with one sack in 11 games, 10 starts). Silvera started eight of 11 contests played in 2021 (38 tackles, 5.5 for loss) and entered the transfer portal after the season. He signed with Arizona State, earning honorable mention All-Pac-12 Conference honors by starting 10 of 12 games played for the Sun Devils (56 tackles, 4.5 for loss with 1.5 sacks, three pass breakups). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Interior plugger set for duties as a nose tackle in a 4-3 front. Silvera is fairly nimble and can get into blockers quickly. He plays with knockback power and can hold his ground against single blockers. He struggles to feel and respond to down blocks. Also, he has trouble reading and reacting to lateral steps looking to seal him behind the play. Silvera has talent and is very active. He could make noise in camp as a late-round pick or priority free agent.
strengths: Above-average short-area athletic ability. | Gets into blocker suddenly, often beating guards to the punch. | Strength to extend an anchor into the gap. | Plays with knockback pop into contact. | Displays a good level of nastiness. | Quick to run feet through contact for bull-rush momentum.
weaknesses: Gets beaten to lateral positioning too often. | Takes time to rid himself of the blocker. | Rush production has been disappointing. | Has trouble transitioning to a second move.

bio: Jones was a three-star recruit from Michigan’s Southfield A&T High School when signing with the Cardinals, making a strong impression in 2019 (18 tackles, four pass breakups in 12 games, two starts). He started once in eight appearances in 2020 (six tackles) and then began three of six games played in 2021 (17 tackles, one interception, three pass breakups) before suffering a season-ending injury. Jones made the most of his senior season, receiving second-team All-MAC platitudes after tying for the BSU lead with 12 pass breakups, intercepting two passes and posting 23 tackles in 11 games with nine starts. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Jones is a long cornerback with average speed but a natural feel for making plays on the football. He’s more confident and consistent at maintaining his feel for the route from press than from off-man. Jones plays with a lane-jumping mentality in off coverage when flat-footed but could succumb to double moves in the pros. Shoddy tackling will work against him, but teams will appreciate his ability to challenge punts and kicks off the edge. Jones might find work as a backup in a press-heavy scheme if he tests well.
strengths: Good size with above-average length. | Squats and jabs receivers square with punch from press. | Effective rerouting and altering timing of the route. | Possesses ballhawking readiness with eyes forward. | Races into the passing lane once route recognition sets in. | Reads eyes and attacks hands with back to the ball. | Blocked a kick and punt during his Ball State career.
weaknesses: Feet are quick but unfocused matching the release. | Allows too much separation chasing route breaks. | Lacks desired fluidity needed in off-man coverage. | Declares hips prematurely, creating recovery situations. | Fails to locate the throw on deep verticals. | Not always a reliable run supporter.

bio: Anderson joined Jones College after playing at Vicksburg High School, leading the team with 74 tackles and earning honorable mention honors on the Junior College All-American team his freshman year. He moved on to Tulane the next season and was productive despite only starting once in 2019 (26 tackles, two for loss in 13 games) and 2020 (88 tackles, 10.5 for loss with 3.5 sacks in 12 contests). Anderson started seven of 11 appearances in 2021 (56 tackles, 8.5 for loss with four sacks) and then was a second-team All-American Athletic Conference pick in 2022 (113 tackles, seven for loss with two sacks, four pass breakups, two forced fumbles in 14 starts). -- by Chad Reuter
overview: It would be easy to write off Anderson due to his stature, but he’s compact, strong and has the skill set to play the linebacker position. He plays with instincts and discipline. He can tackle what is in front of him and can compete for third down and special teams reps. Anderson might have a limited ceiling but he’s a productive football player.
strengths: Plays the game with urgency, intelligence and passion. | Sifts through traffic with patience to locate football. | Mirrors runner’s lane choice with leverage in his scrapes. | Adequate pursuit speed and field agility. | Capable of dropping into coverage or handling man-coverage duties. | Productive tackler on special teams during his career.
weaknesses: Lacks desired height and length. | Must improve ability to slip blocks on the next level. | Big bodies can wash him away on the second level. | Shorter arms put him on the wrong side of missed tackles.

bio: Broeker (pronounced BRO-kurr) was a four-star recruit from Sacred Heart-Griffin High School in Springfield, Illinois, before making his way to Oxford. He earned quite a bit of playing time as a true freshman, suiting up in all 12 games as a key reserve and seeing more than 30 snaps in most games. Broeker started all 10 games of the Rebels' 2020 season and all 13 games in 2021. He slid in to play left guard in 2022, garnering second-team All-SEC accolades after not allowing a single sack in 435 pass-blocking snaps in his 13 starts, per PFF. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Guard prospect with average size who has the ability to punch above his weight as a run blocker. Broeker is limited as a move blocker but thrives when firing out and running his feet through contact to open lanes. He has very strong hands and consistently works to finish his blocks. His hand usage and inconsistent body control land his pass protection a few notches below his run blocking and those issues will take time to clean up. Broeker is a below-average athlete with above-average play strength and has the talent to become a starting guard in a downhill run scheme.
strengths: Treats opponents like a blocking sled once he’s centered up. | Sustains attack with vice grips for hands. | All-day worker and block finisher. | Efficient with hands and hips to swivel and seal cross-face block. | Takes appropriate angles up to second-level targets. | Impressive recovery quickness against sudden movement at the line. | Can sink a sudden anchor with flexible lower half. | Looks for work when uncovered in protection.
weaknesses: Below average length. | Lacks desired athleticism as move blocker. | Entry point can be too tall into his down blocks. | Must learn to play with tighter, inside hands. | Below average win rate landing first hands. | Needs to play with better poise and control in pass sets. | Chases and voids his gap too easily.

bio: Hampton was an all-region pick at Westside High School in South Carolina before redshirting with the Mountaineers in 2018 (two tackles in three games played as a reserve). He played in all 14 games in 2019, racking up 6.5 tackles for loss, 5.5 sacks, 24 tackles, two forced fumbles in one start. Hampton started six on 10 games played in 2020 (42 tackles, 6.5 for loss with three sacks) before bursting onto the national scene as a junior in 2021, garnering third-team All-Sun Belt Conference honors (69 tackles, 17.5 for loss with 11 sacks, two pass breakups in 14 starts). He led the team with 9.5 tackles for loss and registered seven sacks, 39 tackles and three forced fumbles in nine starts in 2022. He earned first-team all-league notice despite missing three games due to injury. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Undersized 3-4 outside linebacker who might require a game plan from his drafting team due to the strengths and weaknesses of his frame and his game. Hampton isn’t anything special as a run defender, but his pass-rush tape really stands out. He’s an explosive, linear pass rusher featuring subtle techniques near the top of the rush that help him access the pocket. Hampton will be a strong tester but finding a clean positional fit could be a challenge. At worst, he could find snaps as a full-time special-teamer and backup linebacker with pass-rush talent.
strengths: Has a history of making high-motor, high-impact plays. | Rare wingspan allows him to stick and separate from blocks. | Explosive lower body with above-average strength for his size. | Expansive tackle net in space. | Possesses an assortment of attacks at the top of the rush. | Sudden, crisp two-hand swipes help clear tackle’s initial punch. | Can lean and rip or use ghost technique to grease the edge. | Keeps feet moving through contact to turn the corner on protection.
weaknesses: Frame might be maxed out. | Below average physical traits to set strong edges. | Needs to play with a greater deal of grit and resistance versus run blockers. | Pursuit burst from change of direction takes time. | Slows feet and grabs rather than running through tackle tries. | Will need to develop inside rush counters.

bio: Herbig is a Hawaii native who played at the famed Saint Louis School in Honolulu, which produced NFL players like Marcus Mariota and Tua Tagovailoa, among others. His brother, Nate, played on the offensive line at Stanford before heading to the league. Nick was the Hawaii Open Division Defensive Player of the Year as a senior and a four-star recruit before coming to Wisconsin. In his first year on campus, he started all seven games and led the Badgers with six tackles for loss (including one sack among 26 tackles). Herbig was an honorable mention All-Big Ten Conference pick in 2021, pacing the team with nine sacks (among 64 tackles, 14.5 for loss). With Leo Chenal off to the NFL in 2022, Herbig became the team's top playmaker, garnering third-team Associated Press All-American and first-team all-conference accolades (47 tackles, 15.5 for loss with 11 sacks, two pass breakups in 11 games) as his sack total tied for sixth in the FBS. He opted out of the team's bowl game to prepare for the draft. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: A three-year starter as a 3-4 outside linebacker, Herbig is lacking in size and strength but possesses plenty of athleticism and potential. He can be a slippery rusher with subtle hands and a wicked inside move that leaves tackles in the mud. His lack of play strength limits his speed-to-power rush and his ability to stand his ground against tackles looking to widen him off the mark. He would benefit from a year in the weight room to get ready for NFL edge work, but he might have the instincts and athletic ability for consideration as an off-ball linebacker.
strengths: More than 26 percent of his career tackles resulted in lost yardage. | Fluid inside move fueled by long, easy strides. | Excellent lower body flexion to dip and flatten into the pocket. | Finds second gear to close and finish quarterbacks. | Plays with good pre-snap recognition of hazards. | Uses hands effectively to stay clean and pursue the football. | Cross-faces tackle and disrupts run plays into the B-gap. | Good agility and change of direction in coverage space.
weaknesses: Angular frame will require additional muscle mass. | Below average play strength and ruggedness at the point of attack. | Unable to sink and set a firm edge. | Lacks lower body strength to push through redirection. | Speed-to-power rush fizzles out. | Would benefit from varied entry angles and tempos as a rusher.

bio: Saldiveri started 11 games at right tackle as a redshirt freshman. The Monarchs did not play due to COVID-19 concerns in 2020, but he came back to garner honorable mention All-Conference USA accolades as a 13-game starter at right tackle in 2021. Saldiveri started all 12 games in 2022 (one at right guard and 11 at right tackle) to earn second-team All-Sun Belt Conference honors. -- by Chad Reuter
overview: Three-year starter with good overall size/length and the potential to play multiple spots along the offensive line. Saldiveri is naturally athletic and should fit best as a zone blocker or pulling guard who can get out into space and find work. Hand skill and placement are consistent issues on tape and could prevent him from neutralizing NFL opposition at a functional level. If he proves he can snap the ball and makes a move to center, that should improve his draft stock and give him a better chance as a pro.
strengths: Football IQ helps him sort through movement and alter assignments if necessary. | Agility and redirection to catch moving targets on second level. | Accelerates and charges through down blocks with choppy feet. | Makes himself longer by effectively counter punching in pass sets. | Easy lateral slides versus rush counters. | Keeps pads squared as long as possible versus edge rushers. | Athletic tools to be an active participant in screen game.
weaknesses: Fails to engage and command the rep through the whistle. | Hands land outside opponents’ pads and slide off the mark. | Slow hand resets to battle for leverage. | Average core strength diminishes drive blocking ability. | Needs to squeeze inside gaps more consistently in pass pro. | Not much punch and separation in protection.
